title: Chiral Quantum Groups and Holography
subtitle: Measuring a field from its boundary

parts.title: Measurements at the boundary
parts.summary: Fix the unit of energy by the first harmonic on a circle. At energy two, one quantum of the second harmonic and two quanta of the first give distinct occupation states. Prepare their normalized sum, then their normalized difference. A count of the quanta gives either occupation with probability one half in both preparations. An operator that exchanges the two occupations, however, has eigenvalue plus one on the sum and minus one on the difference. Can the modes of a local field realize this measurement?

parts.title: Duality and actions on states
parts.summary: Keep three closed fields \(a,b,c\) in that order and bring them together. Suppose the two products differ by the differential of an element \(h\), so that \((ab)c-a(bc)=dh\). They give the same class in cohomology. Place a fourth closed field \(x\) to their right. Now one of the ways of moving the parentheses multiplies \(h\) by \(x\). Knowing the common class of the first two products tells us nothing about the choice of \(h\) for this step. What must an action on states remember when it composes such moves?

parts.title: Combining and sewing operations
parts.summary: Expand the product of two lines in their inverse separation. When a third line is present, suppose each successive coefficient uses a new independent state of that third line. Every finite truncation uses finitely many of its states. Can the third line be adjoined after expanding the pair if the full series uses infinitely many of them? Cut a four-punctured sphere along a circle with two punctures on each side. Each side gives an amplitude that can be evaluated on a state at the cut. Sewing pairs the two amplitudes. With one basis state, this means multiplying their values on it and dividing by its bilinear pairing with itself, provided that pairing is nonzero. With a whole tower of intermediate states, when does the sum converge?

parts.title: Quantum groups, geometry and arithmetic
parts.summary: What current acts on a pair of independently prepared systems? Suppose each carries a current whose self-product has double pole \(1/(z-w)^2\). In the product of the sum with itself there are four terms. The two mixed products are regular, so the coefficient of the double pole is two. A rule sending a current to the sum of its actions must therefore also say what happens to its level. In the geometric examples one can ask the converse question. How much of an algebra of fields can one recover from the rule for combining its sectors?

parts.title: Reconstructing the bulk
parts.summary: In a two-dimensional space choose a basis of states \(u,v\). One operation fixes both. A second sends \(u\) to \(u+v\) and fixes \(v\). Both have trace two, yet applying them to \(u\) distinguishes them. Can a boundary insertion distinguish bulk operations in the same way? For the cubic potential \(W=x^3\), the bulk field \(x\) is nonzero but acts by zero on the cohomology of one boundary. Three insertions of an odd field on that boundary still detect the cubic coefficient. Recovering the missing bulk field asks for another operation.

chapters.title: Boundary observables and reconstruction
chapters.summary: A coupling to the off-diagonal exchange reads a relative phase. Two preparations have the same occupation probabilities. On these two states the current modes give twice the exchange. A joint measurement therefore reads \(+2\) on the sum and \(-2\) on the difference. A disk statistic has the same two means and variance \(28\). On a free-fermion ring the curvature of the energy spectrum supplies a third test. These calculations distinguish preserving a joint observable from preserving all measurements or an absolute amplitude.

chapters.title: Algebras, modules and combining systems
chapters.summary: For an ordinary probe algebra the Chevalley–Eilenberg coupling equation is precisely the bracket relation defining a representation. On two lines with scalar labels \(2\) and \(3\), two actions of the same polynomial generator give \(5\) and \(6\). A coproduct specifies how to combine the actions. For Ising spin lines the possible junctions must also agree on an intermediate sector. Tensoring over its algebra retains six of sixteen pairs.

chapters.summary: The cutting differential expresses the consistency equation for couplings and for the homotopies witnessing their relations. Contract either adjacent pair in a three-letter word. Encoding the operations in one bar differential makes their signs calculable. For connected coefficients with consecutive cuts, at most \(n\) positive factors fit in arity \(n\), which makes reconstruction by cobar finite in each arity.

chapters.title: Recovering interactions from boundary operations
chapters.summary: In a fixed boundary coordinate the cubic and quartic potentials first obstruct extension at different orders. A two-state boundary has the same binary product for \(W=x^3\) and \(W=x^4\). A third insertion distinguishes the two potentials. The identity defect recovers the bulk Jacobi algebra, while a numerical sphere amplitude also needs a trace. On the celestial line the axion Ward identity fixes a coefficient of the simple pole at cubic order in the axion coupling. For the marked pure \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) theory with one axion, fix the cubic brackets covariant under the linear transverse \(\mathrm{SL}_2\) and the ordered three-field residues. In the quartic double pole of \(J_e[x^2]\) with \(J_f[y^2]\), both outgoing negative currents have constant transverse label. Raising the first label to \(x^3\) gives a simple pole that distinguishes which outgoing current carries the derivative. The quartic Ward identities hold for currents with polynomial labels of every transverse degree and for all their longitudinal derivatives. Ordered normal monomials in the four towers and their derivatives, with \(E[1]\) omitted, form a free basis over \(\mathbb C[s]/(s^5)\). The microscopic currents, the separate graph amplitudes, higher orders in \(s\) and a physical two-line coproduct remain to be determined. The scalar bracket on polynomial Hamiltonians acquires a compatible ordered product after adjoining the calibrated square root.

terms.label: Algebra
terms.definition:
**Definition (unital associative algebra).** An algebra \(A\) over \(k\) consists here of a vector space, a bilinear multiplication \(m:A\otimes A\to A,\ a\otimes b\mapsto ab\), and an element \(1_A\) with
\[
 (ab)c=a(bc),\qquad 1_Aa=a=a1_A.
\]
For operators, the identity transformation supplies \(1_A\) and composition supplies the associative product. The scalar multiple \(c\,1_A\) defines the unit map \(u_A:k\to A\). An abstract product acquires this operational meaning once we choose its action on a space of states.

terms.label: Module
terms.definition:
**Definition (left module).** A representation of \(A\), or left \(A\)-module, is a vector space \(M\) with a linear action \(A\otimes M\to M,\ a\otimes v\mapsto av\), satisfying
\[
(ab)v=a(bv),\qquad 1_Av=v.
\]
Thus assigning the operator \(\rho_M(a):v\mapsto av\) to \(a\) gives a unital algebra map \(\rho_M:A\to\operatorname{End}_k(M)\), the algebra of linear operators on \(M\). A map of modules, or *intertwiner*, is a \(k\)-linear map \(f:M\to N\) that transports states compatibly with every action. Its defining equation \(f(av)=af(v)\) compares acting on the input \(v\in M\) and on its image in \(N\).

terms.label: Coproduct
terms.definition:
There is a way to specify such a prescription independently of the representations. If \(H\) acts on \(M\) and \(N\), an element \(a\otimes b\) of \(H\otimes H\) already acts on \(m\otimes n\) by \(am\otimes bn\). For the additive rule assign \(x\otimes1+1\otimes x\) to \(x\), and for the multiplicative rule assign \(x\otimes x\). More generally assign a tensor to each \(h\in H\) and let it act in this way.

Write such a map as
\[
\Delta:H\longrightarrow H\otimes H,
\]
and set
\[
h\cdot(m\otimes n)
=\sum h_{(1)}m\otimes h_{(2)}n,
\qquad
\Delta(h)=\sum h_{(1)}\otimes h_{(2)}.
\tag{2.1}
\]
In this **Sweedler notation** the subscripts distinguish the left and right components of each summand. Acting component by component is bilinear, so the result depends only on the tensor \(\Delta(h)\). There remains the question whether composing two of these operators represents the product in \(H\).

terms.label: Bialgebra
terms.definition: **Definition (bialgebra).** A bialgebra \(H\) is a unital associative algebra with unital algebra maps \(\Delta:H\to H\otimes H\) and \(\epsilon:H\to k\) satisfying coassociativity (2.3) and the two counit identities (2.4). The map \(\Delta\) is its coproduct and \(\epsilon\) its coalgebra counit. In the two polynomial examples above the neutral one-dimensional system has \(x=0\) for the additive rule and \(x=1\) for the multiplicative rule. These are the respective values of \(\epsilon(x)\).

terms.label: Braiding
terms.definition:
**Definition (braiding).** A braiding on a monoidal category is a natural family of isomorphisms
\[
\beta_{M,N}:M\otimes N\longrightarrow N\otimes M,
\]
compatible with tensoring in either variable. With parentheses identified by the associator, these two requirements are the hexagon equations
\[
\beta_{L,M\otimes N}
=(\mathrm{id}_M\otimes\beta_{L,N})
(\beta_{L,M}\otimes\mathrm{id}_N),
\tag{2.9}
\]
\[
\beta_{L\otimes M,N}
=(\beta_{L,N}\otimes\mathrm{id}_M)
(\mathrm{id}_L\otimes\beta_{M,N}).
\tag{2.10}
\]
Equation (2.9) takes \(L,M,N\) to \(M,N,L\), either in one move or through \(M,L,N\). Equation (2.10) takes the same initial order to \(N,L,M\), either moving the pair \(L,M\) at once or through \(L,N,M\). Two successive exchanges of the same pair need not return the identity. This distinction matters for lines whose continuation around each other contributes a phase.

terms.label: Associator
terms.definition:
The tensor product also acts on intertwiners. For example \(f\otimes g\) sends \(m\otimes n\) to \(f(m)\otimes g(n)\). In the category of vector spaces, the assignment \((\ell\otimes m)\otimes n\mapsto\ell\otimes(m\otimes n)\) commutes with applying a linear map to any of the three inputs. This is what *natural* means here. In a general category equipped with a tensor product and tensor unit, the corresponding comparison is specified by an **associator**, a natural isomorphism
\[
\alpha_{L,M,N}:(L\otimes M)\otimes N
\longrightarrow L\otimes(M\otimes N).
\]
On three \(H\)-modules the vector-space reassociation is an intertwiner by (2.3). With four modules we can reassociate successive triples in two ways. Both paths go from
\[
((L\otimes M)\otimes N)\otimes P
\quad\text{to}\quad
L\otimes(M\otimes(N\otimes P))
\]
by applying the associator. The shorter route passes through \((L\otimes M)\otimes(N\otimes P)\). The longer first reassociates the innermost \(L,M,N\), then makes two further moves. The pentagon identity equates the two composite maps. A category with this tensor product, natural associator and compatible left and right identifications with its unit is called **monoidal**.

terms.label: Adjunction
terms.definition:
Let \(A\) be another dg algebra and let \(W\) be an \(A\)-\(B\) bimodule. Derived tensor and derived Hom give an adjunction
\[
\Phi=W\otimes_B^{\mathbf L}-:D(B)
\rightleftarrows D(A):
\Psi=\operatorname{RHom}_A(W,-).
\]
Its defining property is the natural equivalence
\[
\operatorname{RHom}_A(\Phi L,M)
\simeq\operatorname{RHom}_B(L,\Psi M).
\]
**Definition (unit and counit).** The unit \(\eta_L:L\to\Psi\Phi L\) is the image of \(1_{\Phi L}\) under this equivalence. The counit \(\varepsilon_M:\Phi\Psi M\to M\) is the inverse image of \(1_{\Psi M}\). On degree-zero inputs the unit sends \(l\) to the map \(w\mapsto w\otimes l\), and the counit evaluates \(w\otimes f\mapsto f(w)\). For complexes these formulas use resolutions and the sign for interchanging homogeneous inputs. In the involution example the first map identifies \(L\) with the fixed vectors of its trivial representation. The second includes the fixed vectors in \(M\).

The two triangle identities are
\[
\varepsilon_{\Phi L}\circ\Phi(\eta_L)=1_{\Phi L},
\qquad
\Psi(\varepsilon_M)\circ\eta_{\Psi M}=1_{\Psi M}.
\]
The first composite evaluates the map just built from \(l\). The second sends a map out of \(W\) back to itself. To see what the unit detects, take a map \(f:K\to L\) in \(D(B)\). Under the adjunction, \(\Phi f\) corresponds to \(\eta_L\circ f:K\to\Psi\Phi L\). Thus the map that \(\Phi\) induces on derived Hom is postcomposition with \(\eta_L\). It is an equivalence for every source \(K\) precisely when \(\eta_L\) is an equivalence. Requiring this for every \(L\) is precisely full faithfulness of \(\Phi\).

In the other direction, take a map \(h:M\to N\) in \(D(A)\). Under the adjunction, \(\Psi h\) corresponds to \(h\circ\varepsilon_M:\Phi\Psi M\to N\). Here the map on derived Hom is precomposition with the counit. Testing it against every target \(N\) shows that \(\Psi\) is fully faithful precisely when every \(\varepsilon_M\) is an equivalence. An equivalence of the two whole categories requires both conditions.

terms.definition:

terms.label: Field
Locality
terms.definition:
**Definition (locality).** Two even fields \(A,B\) are local if there is an integer \(N\geq0\) such that
\[
(z-w)^N[A(z),B(w)]=0.
\tag{3.2}
\]
Here the bracket is the commutator \(A(z)B(w)-B(w)A(z)\). For fields of definite parity one uses the graded commutator, inserting the sign \((-1)^{|A||B|}\) on interchanging them. The integer \(N\) may depend on the field pair and must work on *every* input. Locality is an identity of distributions. To give a value to the product at the collision itself, its singular terms must still be treated.

terms.label: Vertex algebra
terms.definition:
**Definition (vertex algebra).** In the even convention used here, a vertex algebra consists of a vector space \(V\), a vacuum vector \(\mathbf1\), a translation operator \(T:V\to V\), and a linear assignment
\[
a\longmapsto Y(a,z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}a_{(n)}z^{-n-1}
\]
of a field to every state \(a\). They satisfy the vacuum and creation identities
\[
Y(\mathbf1,z)=\operatorname{id}_V,
\qquad
Y(a,z)\mathbf1\in a+zV[[z]],
\tag{3.4}
\]
the translation identities
\[
T\mathbf1=0,
\qquad
[T,Y(a,z)]=\partial_zY(a,z)=Y(Ta,z),
\tag{3.5}
\]
and locality for each pair \(Y(a,z),Y(b,w)\). Apply these identities to \(v(z)=Y(a,z)\mathbf1\). Creation gives the initial condition \(v(0)=a\). Translation gives the differential equation \(\partial_z v(z)=Tv(z)\), since \(T\mathbf1=0\). Starting from \(v_0=a\), the successive coefficients satisfy \((r+1)v_{r+1}=Tv_r\). Thus
\[
Y(a,z)\mathbf1=e^{zT}a,
\qquad a=a_{(-1)}\mathbf1.
\]
Taking the constant term recovers the state \(a\) from its field on the vacuum. To turn a vector after several insertions into a scalar amplitude one must also specify a functional or pairing.

terms.label: Lambda bracket
terms.definition:
To read several singular coefficients with one test, pair \(Y(a,t)b\) with \(e^{\lambda t}\,dt\) and take the residue in \(t\). A term \(a_{(n)}b\,t^{-n-1}\) contributes only when it meets the term \(\lambda^nt^n/n!\) of the exponential. Regular powers of \(t\) cannot contribute a residue to this test. The resulting polynomial in the formal variable \(\lambda\) is
\[
[a_\lambda b]=\sum_{n\geq0}\frac{\lambda^n}{n!}a_{(n)}b.
\tag{3.7}
\]
This *\(\lambda\)-bracket* collects the poles with the normalization just derived. For the vacuum field it is zero for every \(b\), although the regular product returns \(b\). The geometric chiral bracket permits Laurent multipliers, so it can also recover that regular coefficient. Beilinson and Drinfeld identify vertex algebras with translation-equivariant chiral algebras on the affine line in *Chiral Algebras*, §0.15. Their Theorem 3.5.10 relates the chiral bracket to the full operator product. [The geometric operation and Laurent multipliers](04-factorization.md#lie-and-operator-product)

terms.label: Differential module
terms.definition:
On a smooth complex algebraic curve \(X\) write \(\mathcal O_X\) for the regular functions and \(\mathcal D_X\) for their sheaf of algebraic differential operators. In a coordinate the basic relation is
\[
[\partial_z,z]=1.
\]
A left **differential module**, or left \(\mathcal D_X\)-module, is an \(\mathcal O_X\)-module \(M\) with differentiation obeying the Leibniz rule
\[
\nabla_{\partial_z}(fm)=f'm+f\nabla_{\partial_z}m.
\tag{3.14}
\]
For a vector bundle this is a connection. Differential modules may also be infinite-dimensional or supported on a subvariety, so they include more than vector bundles with connection.

On the coordinate line, a vector space with an operator \(T\) gives the example \(M=\mathcal O_X\otimes V\) with
\[
\nabla_{\partial_z}(f\otimes v)=f'\otimes v+f\otimes Tv.
\]
Indeed a constant section \(1\otimes v\) has derivative \(1\otimes Tv\), and the first term is forced on \(f\otimes v\) by the Leibniz rule. To glue a vertex algebra on arbitrary curves we need in addition the action of changes of formal coordinate. For example, suppose a conformal structure decomposes the state space as a direct sum of eigenspaces of \(L_0\) of nonnegative integral weights. A change of formal coordinate at the origin has a nonzero linear coefficient. First separate this scaling, which acts through the weights. The remaining change is tangent to the identity, with linear term \(z\). Its infinitesimal generators involve only Virasoro modes \(L_m\) with \(m\ge1\). Each lowers weight by at least one. On a state of greatest weight \(d\), every product of more than \(d\) such modes vanishes, so their exponential series terminates. Translation equivariance alone gives the construction on the affine line.

Chiral operations are conventionally written for right differential modules. If \(M\) is a left module, its corresponding right module is
\[
M^{\mathrm r}=\omega_X\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}M,
\]
where \(\omega_X\) is the line bundle of one-forms. In a coordinate,
\[
(dz\otimes m)\cdot\partial_z=-dz\otimes\nabla_{\partial_z}m.
\tag{3.15}
\]
For \(M=\mathcal O_X\) with its ordinary derivative, \((f\,dz)\cdot\partial_z=-f'\,dz\). The sign is forced by integration by parts. For Laurent polynomials \(f,g\), the residue of the exact form \(d(fg)\) vanishes, giving \(\operatorname{Res}f\,dg=-\operatorname{Res}g\,df\). Tensoring with \(\omega_X\) is the equivalence between left and right differential modules. It requires no choice of dual state space.
terms.source_paragraph: A left **differential module**, or left \(\mathcal D_X\)-module, is an \(\mathcal O_X\)-module \(M\) with differentiation obeying the Leibniz rule

terms.label: Configuration space
terms.definition:
**Definition (configuration space).** Let \(X\) be a smooth algebraic curve over a characteristic-zero field \(k\). For a finite nonempty set \(I\), the product \(X^I\) records an \(I\)-labelled family of points. Its open configuration space is
\[
U_I=\{(x_i)\in X^I:x_i\ne x_j\text{ whenever }i\ne j\}.
\tag{4.1}
\]
Write \(j_I:U_I\hookrightarrow X^I\) for its inclusion. The **small diagonal** is the map
\[
\Delta_I:X\longrightarrow X^I,
\qquad x\longmapsto(x)_{i\in I}.
\]
Its image is the locus where all the labelled points coincide. For two labels \(i,j\), the partial diagonal \(\Delta_{ij}\) imposes only \(x_i=x_j\).

terms.label: Chiral operation
terms.definition:
**Definition (chiral operation).** The direct image \(\Delta_{I*}M\) is a differential module on \(X^I\) supported on the small diagonal. It includes derivatives in directions normal to that diagonal. A **chiral \(I\)-operation** is a differential-module map
\[
\mu:
j_{I*}j_I^*\Bigl(\boxtimes_{i\in I}L_i\Bigr)
\longrightarrow\Delta_{I*}M.
\tag{4.3}
\]
Thus its space is
\[
P_I^{\mathrm{ch}}((L_i);M)
=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal D_{X^I}}
\left(j_{I*}j_I^*\boxtimes_iL_i,\Delta_{I*}M\right).
\tag{4.4}
\]
Both sides of the Hom are modules on \(X^I\). Restrict (4.3) to the distinct open for \(|I|>1\) and its target becomes zero. A nonzero operation can therefore only be seen by extending the inputs to the localization and retaining the supported output. This is the operation space of Beilinson–Drinfeld, *Chiral Algebras*, §3.1.1.

terms.label: Factorization algebra
terms.definition:
**Definition (factorization algebra).** In the classical algebraic formulation, a factorization algebra consists of quasi-coherent sheaves \(B_I\) on \(X^I\), together with two kinds of identifications. A surjection \(\pi:J\twoheadrightarrow I\) gives the diagonal identification
\[
\nu_\pi:\Delta_\pi^*B_J\xrightarrow{\sim}B_I
\tag{4.7}
\]
and the factorization identification on the block-separation open
\[
c_\pi:
\left.\boxtimes_{i\in I}B_{J_i}\right|_{U_\pi}
\xrightarrow{\sim}
\left.B_J\right|_{U_\pi}.
\tag{4.8}
\]
The diagonal identifications compose under successive collapses, the open identifications compose under refinements, and restricting a separated product along a diagonal within its blocks agrees with first restricting each block. The \(B_I\) have no nonzero local sections supported on the union of collision diagonals. A unit is a global section \(1\in B_{\{1\}}\) such that the separated product of \(1\) with each local section \(b\) extends to \(B_{\{1,2\}}\) and restricts to \(b\) on the diagonal. These are the ordinary sheaf conditions of *Chiral Algebras*, §§3.4.2–3.4.4.

terms.label: Ran space
terms.definition: The tuples \((x,y)\), \((x,x,y)\) and \((y,x)\) correspond to the same finite subset when \(x\ne y\). The diagonal and relabelling identifications explain why one often describes the compatible family as a sheaf on the **Ran space** of \(X\). At the level of points, this is the set of finite nonempty subsets of \(X\); repeated labels specify the same subset. The maps \(\Delta_\pi\) express exactly those repetitions. One may use the compatible family \((B_I,\nu_\pi)\) without treating the Ran space as an ordinary finite-dimensional variety.

terms.label: Cochain complex
terms.definition:
**Definition (cochain complex).** A cochain complex is a sequence of vector spaces and linear maps
\[
\cdots\longrightarrow V^{n-1}\xrightarrow{d}V^n
\xrightarrow{d}V^{n+1}\longrightarrow\cdots,
\qquad d^2=0.
\]
The superscript is the **cohomological degree**, and the differential has degree \(+1\). A vector killed by \(d\) is a cycle; a vector of the form \(dw\) is a boundary. Their quotient is
\[
H^n(V)=\ker(d:V^n\to V^{n+1})/
\operatorname{im}(d:V^{n-1}\to V^n).
\]
In the two-term target above, \(v\) represents zero in cohomology and \(u\) witnesses that fact. More generally, once \(dw=v\) has a solution, so does \(w+z\) for any cycle \(z\) in the same degree. The set of solutions can therefore matter even after the class of \(v\) has disappeared.

terms.label: Homotopy
terms.definition:
**Definition (cochain homotopy).** A degree-zero chain map \(f:V\to W\) commutes with the differentials. A homotopy from \(g\) to \(f\) is a degree-minus-one map \(h\) satisfying
\[
f-g=d_Wh+hd_V.
\]
If \(x\) is closed, then \((f-g)x=d_W(hx)\). This proves that homotopic maps induce the same map on cohomology. To keep the choice of \(h\), put maps of all degrees into a single complex
\[
\operatorname{Hom}^r(V,W)=\prod_n\operatorname{Hom}(V^n,W^{n+r}),
\qquad
\partial f=d_Wf-(-1)^rfd_V.
\]
Chain maps are its degree-zero cycles, and homotopies identify maps whose difference is a boundary. The product over \(n\) is intentional: a degree-\(r\) map has a component on every degree of \(V\).

terms.label: Quasi-isomorphism
terms.definition: A chain map is a **quasi-isomorphism** if it induces an isomorphism on every cohomology group. The ordinary **derived category** formally makes these maps invertible. We will also retain the derived mapping complexes, obtained by resolving the inputs as necessary, rather than keeping only their degree-zero cohomology. This enhanced form of the derived category remembers homotopies and homotopies between them; it is the meaning intended when the geometric theorem below refers to higher mapping spaces.

terms.label: Massey product
terms.definition:
Changing \(x\) or \(y\) by a degree-one cycle changes \([z]\) by an element of
\([a]H^1(A)+H^1(A)[c]\). In this example \(H^1(A)\) is spanned by \([a],[b],[c]\), and that indeterminacy cannot remove the words \(ay\) and \(xc\). The resulting nonzero coset is a **triple Massey product**. Its degree is \(1+1+1-1=2\), since each primitive lowers the product degree by one. To see what the multiplication table misses, give the algebra \(H^*(A)\) itself zero differential. Its two adjacent products are already zero as elements. Choosing both primitives zero gives the zero coset there.

terms.label: Bar construction
terms.definition:
**Definition (reduced bar construction).** An augmentation of a unital dg algebra is a dg algebra map \(\epsilon:A\to k\), where \(k\) is the ground field. It splits the underlying complex as
\(A=k\cdot1\oplus\bar A\), with \(\bar A=\ker\epsilon\). The **reduced bar construction**, including its empty word, is
\[
BA=T^c(\bar A[1])
=k\oplus\bigoplus_{n\ge1}(\bar A[1])^{\otimes n}.
\]
We write
\[
[a_1|\cdots|a_n]=sa_1\otimes\cdots\otimes sa_n,
\qquad
|[a_1|\cdots|a_n]|=\sum_i|a_i|-n.
\]
The superscript \(c\) indicates the tensor **coalgebra**. Its coproduct splits a word at every position:
\[
\Delta[a_1|\cdots|a_n]
=\sum_{i=0}^n[a_1|\cdots|a_i]
\otimes[a_{i+1}|\cdots|a_n].
\]
The empty word is \(1\). This deconcatenation is coassociative because splitting at two positions gives the same three consecutive subwords in either order. For instance the reduced coproduct of \([a|b|c]\) has the two terms \([a]\otimes[b|c]\) and \([a|b]\otimes[c]\). It retains both places where the triple can be cut.

terms.label: Coherent associative algebra
terms.definition:
**Definition (uncurved \(A_\infty\)-algebra).** Such a structure on \(V\) is a degree-one coderivation \(b\) vanishing on the empty word and satisfying \(b^2=0\). Use \(b_n=-s\,m_n(s^{-1})^{\otimes n}\), with graded tensor products. Thus \(m_n:V^{\otimes n}\to V\) has degree \(2-n\). For \(m_1=d\) and \(ab=m_2(a,b)\) this gives the preceding \(b_1,b_2\), and
\[
 b_3(sa\otimes sb\otimes sc)=(-1)^{|b|}s\,m_3(a,b,c).
\]

terms.label: Conilpotent coalgebra
terms.definition: Deconcatenation on \([a|b|c]\) produces at most three nonempty factors. For a counital coaugmented dg coalgebra \(C=k\oplus\bar C\), write \(1\) for the image of the coaugmentation and \(\bar C\) for the kernel of the counit. On \(c\in\bar C\), remove \(1\otimes c+c\otimes1\) from \(\Delta c\) to obtain the reduced coproduct \(\bar\Delta c\). The coalgebra is **conilpotent** if sufficiently many iterated reduced coproducts kill each element. The three-letter bound illustrates this for the tensor coalgebra.

terms.label: Cobar construction
terms.definition:
**Definition (cobar construction).** The cobar construction is the tensor algebra
\[
\Omega C=T(\bar C[-1]).
\]
Write \(uc\) for a generator in \(\bar C[-1]\), so \(|uc|=|c|+1\). If \(\bar\Delta c=\sum c'\otimes c''\), its differential is the derivation determined by
\[
d_\Omega(uc)=-u(d_Cc)
+\sum(-1)^{|c'|+1}(uc')(uc'').
\]
To check the two signs, take closed degree-zero elements \(a,b\) of the augmentation ideal. The shifted element \([a]\) has degree \(-1\), so its cut contributes \((-1)^{-1+1}=1\). Closedness kills both internal differential terms in \(b[a|b]\). The cobar differential on the generator \(u[a|b]\) is therefore
\[
d_\Omega u[a|b]=-u[ab]+(u[a])(u[b]).
\]
Sending \(u[a]\) to \(a\) and longer single generators to zero takes the displayed boundary to \(-ab+ab=0\). This is the strict counit \(\Omega BA\to A\) on the first multiplication relation. For a coalgebra \(C\), the same check on every generator \(uc\) determines when an assignment of elements of \(A\) extends to a chain map.

terms.label: Twisting cochain
terms.definition:
**Definition (twisting cochain).** A degree-one map \(\tau:C\to A\), vanishing on the coaugmentation and landing in \(\bar A\), is a twisting cochain when
\[
d_A\tau+\tau d_C+\mu_A(\tau\otimes\tau)\bar\Delta=0.
\]
Here \((\tau\otimes\tau)(c'\otimes c'')=(-1)^{|c'|}\tau(c')\otimes\tau(c'')\). This one equation says exactly that \(uc\mapsto\tau(c)\) extends to a dg algebra map \(\Omega C\to A\). For conilpotent \(C\), iterating its reduced coproduct gives the corresponding dg coalgebra map \(C\to BA\). Taking algebra maps that preserve the augmentation and counital coalgebra maps that preserve the coaugmentation gives the strict bar–cobar adjunction
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{\rm dgAlg}(\Omega C,A)
\cong\operatorname{Tw}(C,A)
\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{\rm dgCoalg}(C,BA).
\]
The identities correspond to the strict counit \(\Omega BA\to A\) just tested on \(u[a|b]\), and the strict unit \(C\to B\Omega C\). In the latter map a one-letter component records \(c\) and the longer components record its successive reduced coproducts. Conilpotence makes the word sum finite on each element. An adjunction alone gives no inverse to either comparison.

terms.label: K-flat and K-injective
terms.definition: A right dg module \(P\) is **K-flat** if \(P\otimes_B X\) is acyclic whenever the left dg module \(X\) is acyclic. Such a module computes derived tensor on arbitrary coefficients. Dually, a complex \(J\) is **K-injective** if its Hom complex from every acyclic complex is acyclic. This condition concerns the whole complex; injectivity of each term alone does not suffice in the unbounded case. See the [Stacks Project, §13.31](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/070G).

terms.label: Smooth affine module
terms.definition:
**Definition (smooth affine module).** An \(A_\ell\)-module is smooth if each vector is annihilated by \(t^N\mathfrak g[t]\) for some \(N\), which may depend on the vector. To test the vectors killed by *all* strictly positive modes in a smooth module, induce the trivial \(\mathfrak n\)-module to obtain
\[
W=A_\ell\otimes_{U(\mathfrak n)}\mathbb C.
\]
An affine map \(W\to M\) is determined by the image of \(1\otimes1\), and each vector of \(M\) killed by \(\mathfrak n\) gives such a map. The Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt theorem identifies the underlying vector space of \(W\) with \(H\). Its energy-zero part is the regular \(R\)-module. This distinguishes \(W\) from the scalar-top vacuum
\[
V=A_\ell\otimes_{U(\mathfrak g[t])}\mathbb C,
\]
whose generating vector is also killed by every zero mode. Its energy-zero part is \(\mathbb C\). Derived maps from \(W\) compute the higher positive-current invariants. Precomposition gives those maps their coefficient action.

terms.label: Raw affine level
terms.definition:
Let \(\mathfrak g\) be a nonzero finite-dimensional simple complex Lie algebra. Choose an invariant form \(\kappa\), normalized so that long roots have squared length two, and write
\[
\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}x\,\operatorname{ad}y)
=h^\vee\kappa(x,y).
\]
The integer \(h^\vee\) is the dual Coxeter number. For a scalar parameter \(k\), set \(\ell=(-k-h^\vee)\kappa\). The affine mode algebra \(A_\ell\) has relations
\[
[xt^r,yt^q]=[x,y]t^{r+q}
+r\delta_{r+q,0}\ell(x,y)1.
\]
The central generator acts as \(1\). The scalar \(-k-h^\vee\) is the **raw affine level**, the coefficient of the central cocycle in this normalization. Write \(s=-k\) for the **shifted level**, so that the raw scalar level is \(s-h^\vee\). The mode algebra here has no degree derivation. Its internal energy grading assigns energy \(-r\) to \(xt^r\).

terms.label: Localizing subcategory
terms.definition:
Write \(\operatorname{Loc}(W)\) for the smallest full stable subcategory containing \(W\) and closed under arbitrary coproducts and retracts. In the internally graded case use all energy shifts:
\[
\mathscr C=
\begin{cases}
\operatorname{Loc}_{\mathscr S_\ell}(W),&\text{ungraded},\\
\operatorname{Loc}_{\mathscr S_\ell}
\{W\langle r\rangle:r\in\mathbb Z\},&\text{graded}.
\end{cases}
\]
Under the preceding full-unit theorem,
\[
D(B)\simeq\mathscr C.
\tag{6.8}
\]
The source is generated by \(B\), or by all its internal shifts, using semifree resolutions. The left adjoint preserves coproducts and sends these generators to \(W\) and its shifts. Full faithfulness also lifts cones and retracts between image objects. These facts identify the image exactly with \(\mathscr C\).

Take the opening representation again. Every equivariant map from a trivial representation into \(M\) factors uniquely through the invariant line \(\mathbb C(e_0+e_1)\), even though \(M\) also contains the sign line. Now take any smooth complex \(M\) and test it by maps from objects of \(\mathscr C\). Under the full-unit hypotheses of (6.8), the original counit gives the **coreflection** of \(M\) into \(\mathscr C\),
\[
\Phi\Psi M\xrightarrow{\varepsilon_M}M.
\]
This means that for every \(C\in\mathscr C\), it induces an equivalence on derived maps from \(C\). To prove it, the second triangle identity and the full-unit theorem give
\[
\Psi(\varepsilon_M)=\eta_{\Psi M}^{-1}.
\]
The cone of \(\varepsilon_M\) is therefore killed by \(\Psi\). By adjunction all maps to that cone from \(\Phi L\) vanish in every degree. If \(M\) belongs to \(\mathscr C\), both ends of the counit and hence its cone belong to \(\mathscr C\). Taking the cone itself as test source shows that its identity vanishes, so the counit is an equivalence. Conversely, if the counit is an equivalence, it identifies \(M\) with \(\Phi\Psi M\), which belongs to \(\mathscr C\).

terms.label: Compact object
terms.definition: An object is compact in a category if maps from it commute with arbitrary coproducts. The free module \(B\) is compact in \(D(B)\), so \(W\) is compact **inside \(\mathscr C\)**, with all shifts included when graded. Compactness against arbitrary smooth targets would require an additional statement about \(\Psi\) on coproducts in the ambient category.

terms.label: Joint augmentation torsion
terms.definition:
**Definition (joint augmentation torsion).** A smooth module is jointly augmentation-torsion if for each vector \(v\) some whole ideal power \(\mathfrak a^r\) kills \(v\). The exponent may depend on \(v\). Let \(\mathcal T\subset\operatorname{Sm}(A_\ell)\) be this torsion category and set
\[
D_{\mathfrak a}=
\{M\in\mathscr S_\ell:H^q(M)\in\mathcal T
\text{ for every }q\}.
\]
The cellular category \(\mathscr C\) generated by \(W\) and its required shifts lies in \(D_{\mathfrak a}\).

terms.label: Centre
terms.definition:
**Definition (centre).** For a unital associative algebra \(A\) over a characteristic-zero field \(k\), its centre is
\[
Z(A)=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for every }a\in A\}.
\]
For every left \(A\)-module \(M\), a central element gives an \(A\)-linear operator \(m\mapsto zm\), naturally in \(M\). Conversely, every natural endomorphism of the identity functor on \(A\)-modules arises this way. Let \(\eta\) be such an endomorphism and set \(z=\eta_A(1)\) on the regular left module. By left \(A\)-linearity, \(\eta_A(a)=az\). Right multiplication by \(a\) is also a map of left modules. Naturality for this map gives \(\eta_A(a)=za\), so \(z\) is central. For any \(m\in M\), the module map \(A\to M,\ b\mapsto bm\), sends \(1\) to \(m\). Naturality now gives \(\eta_M(m)=zm\).

terms.label: Hochschild cochains
terms.definition:
The left action on the regular module determines the value at \(a\) from the value at \(1\). Right multiplication supplied the other condition in the proof. To impose both actions in a derived calculation, regard \(A\) as a module over its enveloping algebra \(A^e=A\otimes_k A^{\mathrm{op}}\), with \((a\otimes b^{\mathrm{op}})x=axb\). An \(A\)-bimodule map \(A\to A\) is determined by a central element, so
\[
Z(A)=\operatorname{Hom}_{A^e}(A,A).
\]
Replacing Hom by its derived functor gives the Hochschild cochain complex
\[
C^\bullet(A,A)\simeq R\operatorname{Hom}_{A^e}(A,A).
\]
For an ordinary algebra over \(k\), the bar resolution represents this complex by \(C^n(A,A)=\operatorname{Hom}_k(A^{\otimes n},A)\). Its first differentials are
\[
(bz)(a)=az-za,\qquad
(bf)(a_1,a_2)=a_1f(a_2)-f(a_1a_2)+f(a_1)a_2.
\]
Consequently \(HH^0(A)=Z(A)\), while \(HH^1(A)\) consists of derivations modulo inner derivations. Higher degrees retain further compatibility data.

A class represented by a bimodule map \(A\to A[n]\) acts on a derived left module through
\[
M\simeq A\otimes_A^L M
\longrightarrow A[n]\otimes_A^L M\simeq M[n].
\]
Here differentials have degree \(+1\), and \(V[1]^j=V^{j+1}\). The derived centre retains these operations and their coherent compositions. Hochschild cochains carry an \(E_2\)-algebra structure: products are accompanied by homotopies encoding their interchange. On cohomology this includes the cup product and the degree-minus-one Gerstenhaber bracket. An equivalence of underlying complexes alone does not identify those operations. See [Higher Algebra, §5.3.1](https://www.math.ias.edu/~lurie/papers/HA.pdf) and [Gerstenhaber’s construction](https://www.sas.rochester.edu/mth/sites/doug-ravenel/otherpapers/Ger63.pdf).
terms.source_paragraph: Replacing Hom by its derived functor gives the Hochschild cochain complex

terms.label: Actor and pointing
terms.definition:
Call \(F\) an **actor** when it parametrizes operations on another object. To split an insertion into separated pieces one uses disjoint convolution \(\star\) on the full ordered collision atlas. It sums over all ordered bipartitions. At two distinct labelled points its positive part has the summands \(1|2\) and \(2|1\). Its unit \(K\) is concentrated at the empty configuration. To let \(F\) act on a boundary with the same labels, one uses \(\otimes^!\), the extraordinary pullback of the external tensor product along the diagonal. Its unit \(J\) has the local tensor unit at each configuration. [Convolution on the full ordered collision atlas](04-factorization.md#ordered-cut-geometry).

**Definition (pointing).** A pointing on \(F\) is a coherent coalgebra map
\[
u:J\longrightarrow F.
\]
It specifies a vacuum operation together with all its compatibility homotopies.

terms.label: Homotopy fibre
terms.definition:
**Definition (character and pointed action).** A character of \((F,u)\) is a coalgebra map \(g:F\to C\) together with a specified homotopy \(gu\simeq u_B\). An action is a coalgebra map \(\alpha:F\otimes^!C\to C\) together with a specified homotopy \(\alpha(u\otimes^!1_C)\simeq1_C\). Thus inserting the *actor* vacuum must act as the identity on every boundary input. The definition uses the coassociative coalgebra \(F\) and requires no multiplication on it. The spaces retaining these data are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal X(F,u)
&=\operatorname{hofib}_{u_B}\left[
\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Coalg}}(F,C)
\xrightarrow{u^*}\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Coalg}}(J,C)\right],\\
\mathcal A_C(F,u)
&=\operatorname{hofib}_{1_C}\left[
\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Coalg}}(F\otimes^!C,C)
\xrightarrow{(u\otimes^!1_C)^*}\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Coalg}}(C,C)\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
A homotopy fibre records a point upstairs and a path from its image to the specified base point; its higher simplices record the remaining compatibilities.
terms.source_paragraph: A homotopy fibre records a point upstairs and a path from its image to the specified base point; its higher simplices record the remaining compatibilities.

terms.label: Recognition
terms.definition: **Definition (recognition).** For a fixed \((F,u)\) and this two-colour boundary \(C\), recognition means that \(\Theta\) is an equivalence of the complete spaces. The remaining composite would recover \(\alpha\) by first evaluating it on the boundary vacuum and then multiplying by the original boundary input. The required homotopy \(\Theta\Psi(\alpha)\simeq\alpha\) must itself respect the actor pointing, each collision restriction and families of actions. The half-space calculation tested a cochain map on two inputs. Recognition concerns the two coalgebra mapping fibres defined here.

terms.label: Spectator
terms.definition: The Heisenberg test kept a boundary current in place while the exterior input varied. To study more general tensor-source resolutions, keep additional field insertions at labelled positions \(z_1,\ldots,z_r\). These are the **spectators**. A residue can move an auxiliary mark \(w_a\) onto one of them. Whether a form has a primitive depends on the pole orders allowed before and after that collision. Write \(b_j\ge0\) for the basic bound at spectator \(j\), \(N_{ij}\ge0\) for a pair of spectators, and \(\mu\) for the positive odd bound on marked pairs.

terms.label: Coordinatewise tensor completion
terms.definition: How can finite sums approximate this matrix? Give the image the coordinatewise topology inherited from the full matrix space. A test fixes finitely many entries. A diagonal projection onto the first \(m\) coordinates passes every such test against the identity once \(m\) exceeds the largest index tested. The same square truncation approximates any matrix, and the product of the coordinate spaces is complete. Thus the completion contains every matrix. The successive projection ranks show what the tests have ceased to bound.
terms.source_paragraph: How can finite sums approximate this matrix? Give the image the coordinatewise topology inherited from the full matrix space. A test fixes finitely many entries. A diagonal projection onto the first \(m\) coordinates passes every such test against the identity once \(m\) exceeds the largest index tested. The same square truncation approximates any matrix, and the product of the coordinate spaces is complete. Thus the completion contains every matrix. The successive projection ranks show what the tests have ceased to bound.

terms.label: Laurent series
terms.definition:
**Definition (degreewise Laurent completion).** Give the coefficient space \(V\) over \(F\) the discrete topology. The subspaces \(q^m V[[q]]\) are the neighbourhoods of zero in

\[
V((q))=\bigcup_{N\in\mathbb Z}q^N V[[q]].
\]

Here \(V[[q]]=\prod_{j\ge0}Vq^j\). Truncations converge because each prescribed coefficient eventually stabilizes and the omitted tail has order tending to infinity. An element of \(V((q))\) has one lower Laurent bound and an arbitrary sequence of coefficients in \(V\).

terms.label: Relative current complex
terms.definition:
Let \(Z_I=\bigcup_{i<j}\{t_i=t_j,\ z_i=z_j\}\), and let \(\mathcal M_Z\subseteq\mathcal M_I\) consist of currents supported on \(Z_I\). The relative complex is the mapping cone \(\operatorname{Cone}(\mathcal M_Z\hookrightarrow\mathcal M_I)\) with differential

\[
\mathcal F_{\mathcal M}^n
 =\mathcal M_I^n\oplus\mathcal M_Z^{n+1},
\qquad
d_F(\alpha,\gamma)=(\mathcal D\alpha+\gamma,-\mathcal D\gamma).
\]

terms.label: Normalized boundary hypothesis
terms.definition: **Definition (normalized boundary hypothesis).** Fix the displayed trivalent normalization, the measure \(d\nu\), and the local coordinates at the four punctures. Compare the two channel expansions on logarithms continued together from the positive real configurations. For algebraic external states the hypothesis requires that the two four-point inverse-Gram sewings converge in their respective channel discs, that their marked channel vectors lie in the canonical spectral \(L^2\) spaces, and that the specified real unitary fusion transformation relates these vectors. Comparing paths through several changes of channel also uses the normalized positive-label pentagon. The role of quantum-group harmonic analysis in constructing fusion transformations is developed by [Ponsot and Teschner, *Liouville bootstrap via harmonic analysis on a noncompact quantum group*](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9911110); analytic continuation of fusion coefficients alone does not supply every completed-source estimate used here.

terms.label: Determinant line
terms.definition:
**Definition (determinant line).** For the complex \(C\), write \(\det C^j=\bigwedge^{\dim C^j}C^j\). The even-degree top exterior powers and the duals of the odd-degree ones form the line

\[
\operatorname{Det}C
=\bigotimes_j(\det C^j)^{(-1)^j}.
\]

terms.label: Normalized state
terms.definition: Here \(\partial_C\) contracts two observable slots with \(C\); the exponential terminates on a polynomial. The unnormalized functional is \(Z(F)=G_C\omega(F)\). Consequently a state is the normalized linear functional \(\omega\), while an amplitude retains the factor and line in which \(G_C\) lives. Positivity is asserted for the actual even probability law when available; odd integration is algebraic Berezin extraction.

terms.label: Cap
terms.definition: **Definition (cap).** A cap is a chosen filling \(M\) of a boundary, with fields, boundary conditions and normalization preparing a vector or functional in the boundary state space. When amplitudes take values in an anomaly line, specifying that line and its identification across the cut is part of the preparation.

terms.label: Associative chiral algebra
terms.definition:
**Definition (associative chiral algebra).** For either convolution, an associative chiral algebra is an augmented \(E_1\)-algebra \(A\) with positive augmentation ideal whose bar coalgebra \(BA\) factorizes. If \(I=S\sqcup T\) is an admissible decomposition and \(U_{S,T}\) is the open where its two blocks are disjoint, factorization requires the coproduct component to induce an equivalence
\[
(BA)_I|_{U_{S,T}}\xrightarrow{\sim}
     \bigl((BA)_S\boxtimes(BA)_T\bigr)|_{U_{S,T}} .
\]
For \(\star_{\mathrm{cut}}\) the admissible decompositions are the consecutive cuts. For \(\star\) they are all ordered decompositions into subsets. [CQ1](#ref-ch12-cq1)

terms.label: Chiral coproduct
terms.definition:
**Definition (chiral coproduct).** Specify a tensor product \(\diamond\) combining systems at the same positions, together with the geometric interchange that makes \(A\diamond A'\) an algebra for the chosen convolution. An \(E_1\) chiral coproduct is an algebra map
\[
D:A\longrightarrow A\diamond A
\]
with coassociativity and a counit to the \(\diamond\)-unit, or a level-indexed family of such maps. In a derived formulation these include the indicated homotopies and their higher identities. They are not supplied by naming two binary arrows.

terms.label: Spectral form
terms.definition:
**Definition (unitary spectral coquasitriangular form).** A unitary spectral coquasitriangular form is an \(R\)-bilinear map
\[
\rho_z:H\otimes H\longrightarrow R[z,z^{-1}]
\]
with the following identities:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\rho_z(1,a)&=\varepsilon(a)=\rho_z(a,1),\\
\rho_z(ab,c)&=\rho_z(a,c_1)\rho_z(b,c_2),\\
\rho_z(a,bc)&=\rho_z(a_1,c)\rho_z(a_2,b),\\
\rho_z(a_1,b_1)a_2(z)b_2
&=b_1a_1(z)\rho_z(a_2,b_2),\\
\rho_z(Ta,b)&=\partial_z\rho_z(a,b)=-\rho_z(a,Tb),\\
\rho_z(a_1,b_1)\rho_{-z}(b_2,a_2)
&=\varepsilon(a)\varepsilon(b).
\end{aligned}
\]
The fourth identity specifies exchange, and the last makes exchange reversible. A **level** is a Hopf automorphism \(\eta\) commuting with \(T\) and preserving \(\rho_z\). Choose a group \(\Lambda\) of levels, with multiplication given by composition of automorphisms. These data define the spectral class of chiral quantum groups considered here. [CQ2](#ref-ch12-cq2)

terms.label: Contramodule
terms.definition:
**Definition (graded contramodule).** A graded contramodule is a graded vector space \(Q\) with a degree-zero contraaction \(\gamma:\mathbb T_{B_c}(Q)\to Q\) satisfying
\[
\gamma\eta_Q=1_Q,\qquad
\gamma\mathbb T_{B_c}(\gamma)=\gamma m_Q.
\]
Thus \(\gamma\) evaluates the permitted infinite sums. A **curved differential graded contramodule** additionally has a degree-one connection \(D_Q\) satisfying the Leibniz rule for all these sums and
\[
D_Q(bq)=d(b)q+(-1)^{|b|}bD_Q(q),\qquad D_Q^2(q)=hq.
\]
These objects and their graded contramodule maps form the differential graded category \(\operatorname{CDGContra}(B_c)\), with differential \(f\mapsto D_{Q'}f-(-1)^{|f|}fD_Q\) on maps \(Q\to Q'\). An arbitrary \(Q\) is not assigned a topology: its summations are the contraaction, whereas the specified free objects have the displayed inverse-limit topology.

terms.label: Geometric realization
terms.definition:
**Definition (geometric realization).** A geometric realization of the vacuum-marked system consists of \(\mathcal O\)-linear functors
\[
F_I:\mathcal C_I\longrightarrow\operatorname{QCoh}(X^I)
\]
and comparisons with the finite-map functors and separated fusion. Here \(\operatorname{QCoh}\) denotes quasi-coherent sheaves. Define the realized vacuum coefficients
\[
B_I=F_I(v_I).
\]
Require their collision and separated-fusion comparisons to be isomorphisms, and require that \(B_I\) have no nonzero local sections supported on the diagonal divisor. Finally, the empty comparison must identify \(B_\varnothing\) with \(\mathbb C\) **as a unital algebra**. To see the scale this fixes, take the trivial coefficients \(B_I=\mathcal O_{X^I}\) and give a section \(a\) the new coordinate \(2^{|I|-1}a\). At the empty set, coordinates \(x,y\) thus represent the old scalars \(2x,2y\). Their product has new coordinate \(\tfrac12(2x)(2y)=2xy\), so its unit has coordinate \(1/2\). At one point the coordinate is unchanged. Insertion therefore sends \(x\) to \(2x\) and carries the empty algebra unit to the vacuum \(1\). Inserting the vector with coordinate \(1\) would instead give \(2\). [GR1](#ref-ch13-gr1)

terms.label: Ribbon category
terms.definition:
**Definition (ribbon category).** A ribbon category is a rigid braided monoidal category with a twist compatible with duality. For objects \(M,N\), write \(c_{M,N}:M\otimes N\to N\otimes M\) for the exchange and \(\theta_M:M\to M\) for the natural twist. Write \(\mathbf1\) for the tensor unit and \(M^\vee\) for the dual of \(M\). The twist satisfies
\[
\theta_{M\otimes N}
=c_{N,M}c_{M,N}(\theta_M\otimes\theta_N),\qquad
\theta_{M^\vee}=(\theta_M)^\vee,
\]
with \(\theta_{\mathbf1}=1\). The braiding satisfies the hexagons, and the evaluation and coevaluation maps satisfy the duality triangles.

terms.label: Pro-object
terms.definition:
On this affine line, for the principal parts of one Heisenberg current, multiplication by the Vandermonde in the auxiliary variables gives an integral coefficient isomorphism
\[
V_n:F^-_{I,n}\xrightarrow{\sim}F^+_{I,n}.
\]
For the differential with zero central contractions, it extends to the full Cousin complexes, their subcomplexes with positive state count at every block, and the corresponding vacuum quotients. Dualizing requires a specified topology. For a perfect right differential-module complex \(P\), use
\[
P^\sharp=\operatorname{RHom}_{D_{X^I/R}}
(P,D_{X^I/R})^t[|I|],
\qquad t(\partial_{z_i})=-\partial_{z_i}.
\]
For an increasing perfect presentation, retain the inverse system of these duals: a **pro-object**. Finite state, pole and normal-derivative data determine a finite stage; no common finite stage for all states is imposed.

terms.label: Rational-current intertwining map
terms.definition: **Definition (rational-current intertwining map).** An intertwining map is a linear map \(I:W_1(p)\otimes W_2(q)\to\overline X\) satisfying \(I(av)=\iota(a)I(v)\) for every rational current \(a\in\mathfrak g_{\{p,q\}}\) and every input \(v\).

terms.label: Brane and BRST differential
terms.definition:
This preparation takes place in the protected Omega-deformed M-theory on \(\mathbb R_t\times\mathbb C_z\times\mathbb C_w\), whose perturbative bulk action is noncommutative Chern–Simons theory. An M2 brane has two spatial worldvolume dimensions and an M5 has five, each with one time dimension. After the deformation the M2 supplies the line along \(t\). An M5 supplies a chiral surface along \(z\) at fixed \(t,w\). The general line coupling pairs the divided transverse Taylor coefficient \(\partial_z^m\partial_w^n A_t/(m!n!)\) with the generator labelled by \(m,n\). [Gaiotto–Oh, *Aspects of Omega-deformed M-theory*, §§2.7–3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/1907.06495v2)

What relation must two such couplings obey when they act in succession on the same line? Costello's protected M2 theory permits two independent calculations of the answer. Place \(K\) M2 branes at the tip of an \(A_{n-1}\) singularity. The five-dimensional gauge field then takes values in \(\mathfrak{gl}_n\). Write \(c\) for the transverse noncommutativity, so \(z*w-w*z=c\) in the Moyal product, and \(h_{\mathrm b}\) for the bulk loop parameter. Fix \(c\ne0\) and choose units with \(c=1\). Perturbation theory is formal in \(h_{\mathrm b}\).

::: example {#ch14-m2-first-jet-commutator title="Two first jets on an M2 line"}
For \(n\ge2\) let \(E=E_{12}\) send the second basis vector to the first. Write \(J(H)\) for the universal line generator labelled by the matrix-valued polynomial \(H\). Apply the two first-jet operations \(J(Ez)\) and \(J(Ew)\) in opposite time orders and subtract. At tree level their bracket is the matrix commutator with Moyal multiplication of the entries. Both orders contain the matrix factor \(E^2=0\). At one loop the bulk operator product has a second colour contraction. For labels \(E_{ij}z,E_{kl}w\) it leaves the product of the two constant generators \(J(E_{il})J(E_{kj})\). Every other term in the one-loop formula is multiplied by \(\delta_{jk}\) or \(\delta_{il}\). On the chosen pair both deltas vanish, so in the order and normalisation of Costello's (9.3.11) the bulk dual gives
\[
 [J(Ez),J(Ew)]
   =\frac{h_{\mathrm b}}{32\pi^2}\,J(E)^2+O(h_{\mathrm b}^2).
\]
The constant algebra embeds in the classical enveloping algebra by the Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt theorem. In this subalgebra \(U(\mathfrak{gl}_n)\), \(E\) acts on two copies of the defining representation by \(E\otimes1+1\otimes E\). Its square sends \(e_2\otimes e_2\) to \(2e_1\otimes e_1\). Replacing this product by multiplication of the colour matrices would discard a nonzero output. [Costello, §9.3, equation (9.3.11)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1705.02500#page=42)

The brane description begins with two matrices \(B_1,B_2\) acting on \(\mathbb C^K\) and maps \(I:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^K\), \(P:\mathbb C^K\to\mathbb C^n\). The classical equation is \([B_1,B_2]+IP=c\,1_K\), modulo changes of basis in \(\mathbb C^K\). Quantum Hamiltonian reduction gives its protected operator algebra. The generators labelled by transverse monomials come from the framed words \(PB_1^rB_2^sI\) with their colour indices contracted against a matrix. In the presentation valid uniformly in \(K\), interchanging the two first-jet words can join their colour indices or contract their transverse letters. The two colour joins again require \(2=1\). The transverse contraction leaves two constant words, giving \(h_{\mathrm l}J(E)^2\) to first order in the brane parameter \(h_{\mathrm l}\).

At \(K=1\) this contraction is visible in the reduction itself. Write \(D,X\) for the conjugate centre-of-mass operators in the order \([D,X]=h_{\mathrm l}\). They commute with the constant off-diagonal flavour operator \(T\). The corresponding one-letter insertions give
\[
 [TD,TX]=T^2[D,X]=h_{\mathrm l}T^2 .
\]
For a finite numerical example take \(n=2\) and \(c/h_{\mathrm l}=4\). In the ordered reduction the moment equation on the framing variables \(r_1,r_2\) reads \(r_1\partial_{r_1}+r_2\partial_{r_2}+2=c/h_{\mathrm l}\). Thus homogeneous quadratics furnish a flavour module. With \(T=r_1\partial_{r_2}\), the commutator sends \(r_2^2\) to \(2h_{\mathrm l}r_1^2\).

On the uniform algebra, comparing the two first-order coefficients fixes \(h_{\mathrm l}=h_{\mathrm b}/(32\pi^2)\) to first order in these conventions. The reading is an operator coefficient, before choosing a state on the line. [Costello, §§1.5–1.7, Lemma 11.0.1 and §§13.1–13.3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1705.02500#page=56)
:::

Which algebra contains this commutator to every order? On the bulk side, take the Koszul dual at the vacuum augmentation on a time interval times a formal transverse disc, retain the sum of rotation weight spaces at each finite perturbative order and take the inverse limit over those orders. On the brane side, use the algebra of operators uniform in \(K\). Its maps to the finite-\(K\) reductions at nonzero brane parameter are surjective and send the central rank parameter \(\kappa\) to \(K\). Costello's deformation theorem identifies the two completed associative algebras after a formal change of the loop parameter whose higher coefficients may depend polynomially on \(\kappa\). Constructing the bulk dual uses only the bulk fields and their augmentation. The independent M2 comparison comes from the framed matrix reduction and the agreement of its deformation class with the bulk one. The theorem concerns products of protected line operators. Joining two endpoints asks for the actions at the ends of the interval as well. [Costello, §§8 and 13.4, Theorem 16.0.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1705.02500#page=84)

Let the line end on an M5 surface. Operators incident on an endpoint act on its space of states, making that space a module. At a crossing a state \(m\) carries an action from each side. If an insertion \(a\) on the left can pass an insertion \(b\) on the right without changing the state, then \((am)b=a(mb)\). These commuting actions make the crossing states a bimodule. Shrink an interval with an operator at each end. An insertion on the common line can first be moved to the right end of the left piece or to the left end of the right piece. The two answers must agree after joining. In the [fusion channels of the preceding chapter](#ch13-finite-rational-categories-and-a-non-scalar-base) the shared datum was a sector label. At this junction it is the whole action of the operators on the line.

The fields on a brane form the open sector; a field that can be inserted away from the brane belongs to the closed sector. A square-zero supercharge gives differentials on these fields, and the Becchi–Rouet–Stora–Tyutin (BRST) differential implements gauge symmetry with ghost fields. On these complexes, composition can retain a relation among junction operators even if ordinary multiplication forgets it. In the particle model a degree-two class detects the flux of the line. Its proposed realization by integrating the fields on a physical interval requires an independently constructed interval action with both endpoints.

terms.label: Hall correspondence
terms.definition:
**Definition (Hall correspondence).** Let \(\mathcal M_\alpha\) be the moduli stack of objects of charge \(\alpha\) in an abelian category. A charge is an additive class, such as a class in a Grothendieck group. Let \(\mathcal E_{\alpha,\beta}\) classify pairs \(B\subset M\) with quotient of charge \(\alpha\) and subobject of charge \(\beta\). Keeping the two factors, or keeping the middle object, gives the two maps
\[
\mathcal M_\alpha\times\mathcal M_\beta
\xleftarrow{\ p\ }\mathcal E_{\alpha,\beta}
\xrightarrow{\ q\ }\mathcal M_{\alpha+\beta},
\qquad
p(M,B)=(M/B,B),\quad q(M,B)=M.
\]
For rational, isomorphism-invariant constructible functions \(f,g\) of finite charge support over \(\mathbb C\), pull their product back along \(p\) and integrate over the fibre of \(q\). The ordinary Hall product at \(M\) is
\[
(f*g)(M)=\int_{B\subset M}f(M/B)g(B)\,d\chi_c.
\tag{15.1}
\]
On a domain with constructible subobject varieties, stratify the fibre into finitely many pieces on which \(f(M/B)g(B)\) has constant value. Multiply each value by the compactly supported Euler characteristic of its piece and add. The indicator of the zero object is the unit. The order in (15.1) is quotient first, subobject second.

terms.label: Orientation root
terms.definition:
**Definition (orientation root).** To glue these coefficient complexes, fix a line \(J_F\) on the moduli problem with an isomorphism from its tensor square to the self-extension determinant at \(F\). Write
\[
K_F=\det R\operatorname{Hom}(F,F),\qquad
D(F,G)=\det R\operatorname{Hom}(F,G),\qquad
J_F^{\otimes2}\simeq K_F.
\]
Already for a split extension the root map takes \(J_F\otimes J_G\otimes D(F,G)\) to \(J_{F\oplus G}\). Its square is the determinant identification for the direct sum. For a flag the corresponding maps must be compatible on exact triangles. Taking only an Euler-characteristic sign loses the cross determinant line \(D(F,G)\) that occurs in these maps.

terms.label: Semi-topological component
terms.definition:
For a compact orientation example take \(X=S_{\mathrm{Kum}}\times E\), where \(S_{\mathrm{Kum}}\) is a smooth projective Kummer K3 surface and \(E\) an elliptic curve. Fix a Calabi–Yau volume form, a smooth elliptic fibre \(C\subset S_{\mathrm{Kum}}\) meeting a divisor in degree one, points \(p\in C\), \(x\in E\), and \(L\in\operatorname{Pic}^0(E)\). The actual semi-topological components of
\[
A=\mathcal O_C\boxtimes\mathcal O_x,
\qquad B=\mathcal O_p\boxtimes L
\]
generate a subgroup \(\Gamma\cong\mathbb Z^2\). Here a semi-topological component is a connected-component class in the moduli of perfect complexes, with addition induced by direct sum. The two degree-four Chern characters lie in distinct Künneth summands, so the two component classes are independent. On the union of components indexed by \(\Gamma\), the Joyce–Upmeier compact orientation root with its prescribed square admits unital associative root maps for every finite ordered flag with graded terms in this union. The two isomorphism classes of enhancements form an \(H^2(\Gamma,\mathbb F_2)\)-torsor. [Strong orientation on compact two-charge components][strong-orientation]

terms.label: Rigidification
terms.definition:
Rigidifying the residual central \(\mu_n\) and dividing by the translation subgroup \(E[n]\) defines
\[
\mathfrak R_n^{\mathrm{amb}}
=\bigl[(\mathfrak V_n\mathbin{/\mkern-6mu/}\mu_n)/E[n]\bigr].
\]
The derived stack \(\mathfrak R_n^{\mathrm{amb}}\) has a closed nondegenerate \((-1)\)-shifted symplectic form and smooth classical truncation
\[
\mathcal B_n=[(C_n\mathbin{/\mkern-6mu/}\mathbb G_m)/E].
\]
The double slash denotes rigidification: locally the objects are retained while their central scalar automorphism subgroup is quotiented out. The corresponding lifting gerbe is the stack of local choices of a lift, with their scalar automorphisms; it is not just a set of choices. The cyclic formal neighbourhoods of \(\mathfrak R_n^{\mathrm{amb}}\) agree with those of \(T^*[-1]\mathcal B_n\). A global algebraic equivalence is known at length one; formal agreement at general length does not assert a global equivalence. Nevertheless, the canonical roots \(K_{\mathcal B_n}\) identify the critical coefficients with \(\mathscr P_n=\mathbb Q_{\mathcal B_n}[0]\). On the common-lifting classical flag stack the resulting map \(p^*(\mathscr P_a\boxtimes_{BE}\mathscr P_b)\to q^!\mathscr P_{a+b}\) is an isomorphism with zero source shift; \(BE\) is the classifying stack of elliptic-curve torsors. These give actual classical Hall arrows at every positive length, compatible with the full ordered flags. [Elliptic Weyl transport, ambient paired reduction and critical coefficients][spherical-reduction]

terms.label: Stable pair
terms.definition: The sphere can distinguish two products with equal closed traces. We can nevertheless ask for the closed traces themselves, for all primitive classes at once. A second description of the counted curves uses a stable pair on \(X=S\times E\). This is a morphism \(\mathcal O_X\to F\) with \(F\) pure of dimension one and zero-dimensional cokernel. Purity means that \(F\) has no nonzero zero-dimensional subsheaf. For a primitive effective K3 class \(\beta_h\) of square \(2h-2\), the reduced Donaldson–Thomas and stable-pair theories have a common rational function \(R_{h,d}(v)\). Its Laurent expansion at \(v=0\) gives their series.

terms.label: Weil functional
terms.definition:
Use logarithmic scale \(u=\log x\), so multiplication of positive scales becomes addition. For a test \(f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)\), set
\[
\widehat f(z)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(u)e^{izu}\,du,
\qquad
H_f(s)=\int_{\mathbb R}f(u)e^{(s-1/2)u}\,du
=\widehat f(-i(s-1/2)).
\]
Convolution and involution are
\[
(f*g)(u)=\int f(t)g(u-t)\,dt,
\qquad f^*(u)=\overline{f(-u)}.
\]
**Definition (complete Weil functional).** With Lebesgue measure \(du\) on logarithmic scale and the Fourier sign above, put
\[
\begin{aligned}
W(f)={}&H_f(0)+H_f(1)-f(0)\log\pi\\
&+\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}\widehat f(r)
\operatorname{Re}\psi(1/4+ir/2)\,dr\\
&-\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\Lambda(n)}{\sqrt n}
\bigl(f(\log n)+f(-\log n)\bigr),
\end{aligned}
\tag{16.1}
\]
Here \(\psi=\Gamma'/\Gamma\). The von Mangoldt function is \(\Lambda(p^k)=\log p\) for a prime \(p\) and \(k\ge1\), and vanishes on other integers. The evaluations \(H_f(0),H_f(1)\) are the polar terms. The term at zero and the integral containing \(\psi\) come from the real place. A test concentrated near \(\log4\) selects the positive orientation of the \(2^2\) term calculated above. Reflecting the test selects the other orientation with the same weight. Both tests still have their polar and real-place contributions. [The test algebra and its scalar functional][trace-foundations]

terms.label: Weil positivity
terms.definition:
**Definition (Weil form).** The Hermitian pairing of two complex tests \(f,g\) is \(W(f^**g)\), conjugate-linear in \(f\). Its diagonal is
\[
Q(g)=W(g*g^*).
\tag{16.3}
\]
**Conditional corollary (Weil positivity).** Assuming the Riemann hypothesis, \(Q(g)\ge0\) for every \(g\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)\). Indeed \(\widehat{g*g^*}(z)=\widehat g(z)\overline{\widehat g(\bar z)}\), so (16.2) then sums the nonnegative numbers \(m_\rho|\widehat g(w_\rho)|^2\).

terms.label: Frobenius lift
terms.definition:
A jet at a complex zero records derivatives as well as its scalar value. At a finite prime \(p\) one can ask the corresponding question with integral coefficients, including \(p=2\). Work with \(p\)-torsionfree, \(p\)-complete delta test rings. A Frobenius lift \(\varphi\) is a ring endomorphism reducing to \(x\mapsto x^p\) modulo \(p\). It determines \(\delta(x)=(\varphi(x)-x^p)/p\). On \(\mathbb Z_p\), take \(\varphi=\mathrm{id}\). A point \(a\in\mathbb Z_p\) then gives the height-\(h\) list \(a,\delta a,\ldots,\delta^{h-1}a\). To retain the neighbourhood of such a list, put
\[
A_h=\mathbb Z_p[x_0,\ldots,x_{h-1}],\quad
R_h=\varprojlim_nA_h/p^n,\quad
I_h=(p,x_i^p-x_i:i<h),\quad
B_h=\varprojlim_nA_h/I_h^n.
\]
Here \(R_h\) completes polynomial coefficients \(p\)-adically. The equations \(x_i^p-x_i=0\bmod p\) define all of \(\mathbb F_p^h\), and \(B_h\) completes along this whole locus. For each \(c\in\mathbb F_p^h\), choose the integer representatives \(0\le c_i<p\) in \(\mathbb Z_p\). With these lifts, Chinese remainders give
\[
B_h\simeq\prod_{c\in\mathbb F_p^h}\mathbb Z_p[[z_0,\ldots,z_{h-1}]],
\qquad x_i=c_i+z_i.
\tag{16.13}
\]
For \(h=1,\ p=2\), (16.13) has two factors. In the factor labelled \(0\) the coordinate is \(z=x_0\), and in the one labelled \(1\) it is \(z=x_0-1\). Specifying a function in each factor retains its entire formal dependence on \(z\). Evaluation at the mark instead takes a scalar. The map \(j_h:R_h\to B_h\) is injective, also modulo each \(p^n\). Indeed translation by any chosen \(c\) is a polynomial automorphism, and a polynomial over \(\mathbb Z/p^n\) injects into the corresponding formal power-series ring.

Frobenius has the variance
\[
\varphi_h:R_h\longrightarrow R_{h+1},
\qquad x_i\longmapsto x_i^p+px_{i+1}.
\]
It raises height. Its extension to \(B_h\to B_{h+1}\) commutes with \(j\). At the arithmetic point \(a\), evaluate \(x_i\) at \(\delta^i(a)\). This evaluation commutes with Frobenius because \((\delta^i a)^p+p\delta^{i+1}a=\delta^ia\); it does not preserve all normal operations.

To define the normal operation, let \(S_i(x,y)\) be the integral arithmetic addition polynomials, characterized by the free-jet identity \(S_i(x,y)=\delta^i(x_0+y_0)\). The first two are
\[
S_0=x_0+y_0,\qquad
S_1=x_1+y_1-
\frac{(x_0+y_0)^p-x_0^p-y_0^p}{p}.
\]
The quotient polynomial is integral. Use independent divided-power parameters \(t_i\); their symbols \(t_i^{[n]}\) satisfy \(t_i^{[r]}t_i^{[s]}=\binom{r+s}{r}t_i^{[r+s]}\), so the construction does not invert factorials in \(\mathbb Z_p\). Congruence translation is the coaction
\[
\alpha(x_i)=S_i(x,pt).
\]
It extends continuously to the rational-locus completion because it preserves its defining ideal. Extracting the coefficient of \(t_0^{[1]}\) defines the first normal derivation \(D_0\). For \(h\ge2\), in the first two coordinates,
\[
D_0x_0=p,\qquad D_0x_1=-px_0^{p-1}.
\]
The point relation \(h_0=x_0^p+px_1-x_0\) therefore obeys
\[
\operatorname{ev}_a(h_0)=0,
\qquad D_0h_0=p^2x_0^{p-1}-p^2x_0^{p-1}-p=-p.
\tag{16.14}
\]
At height two and \(p=2\) this says \(h_0=x_0^2+2x_1-x_0\) vanishes at every pair \((a,\delta a)\), whereas \(D_0h_0=-2\equiv2\bmod 4\). Thus the ideal of functions vanishing at the arithmetic points is not stable under the first normal derivation. The formal factors in (16.13) retain the missing direction.

terms.label: Commutator quotient
terms.definition: **Definition (commutator quotient).** For an algebra \(A\) over \(R=\mathbb Z_p\), let \([A,A]_R\) be the \(R\)-linear span of the elements \(UV-VU\), for \(U,V\in A\). The quotient module \(HH_0(A/R)=A/[A,A]_R\) is the relative zeroth Hochschild homology. Every cyclic \(R\)-linear map from \(A\) factors uniquely through this module. The distinction from a two-sided ideal matters already on the disk above. Since \([d,z]=2\), the ideal generated by the commutators contains \(2zd\), on which the trace modulo four takes the value \(2\).

terms.label: Proper trace ideal
terms.definition:
**Definition (trace-class endomorphisms of the theta complex).** For Hilbert spaces \(H,K\), write \(\mathfrak S_1(H,K)\) for the operators \(H\to K\) whose singular values have finite sum, and \(\mathfrak S_1(H)=\mathfrak S_1(H,H)\). The identity on an infinite-dimensional space has singular value one in every direction. For \(\mathscr C_s=[V\to U]\) the proper trace domain has two degrees,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathfrak I^0&=\{(T^{-1},T^0)\in\mathfrak S_1(V)\oplus\mathfrak S_1(U):
dT^{-1}=T^0d\},\\
\mathfrak I^{-1}&=\mathfrak S_1(U,V).
\end{aligned}
\]
Composition and \(\delta\) make \(\mathfrak I\) a complete proper nonunital differential ideal of the bounded degree-zero chain maps and degree-minus-one homotopies. Its closed graded trace is zero in degree minus one and satisfies
\[
\tau(T)=\operatorname{Tr}_UT^0-\operatorname{Tr}_VT^{-1},
\qquad \tau(\delta K)=0.
\]
The last identity follows from \(\operatorname{Tr}(dK)=\operatorname{Tr}(Kd)\). Orthogonal splitting of the closed range of \(d\) contracts this ideal onto \(\mathfrak S_1(K_s)\) by a split differential-algebra quasi-isomorphism. The chain-map equation involves \(d\), whereas taking ordinary Hilbert adjoints involves \(d^*\); a positive differential-star structure does not follow. [Trace-class coefficient homotopies][trace-operations]

terms.label: Interface
terms.definition: **Definition (interface bimodule).** In the algebraic model of a defect between differential graded algebras \(A\) and \(B\), the interface is a complex \(P\) with commuting left \(A\)- and right \(B\)-actions compatible with its differential. It carries a left \(B\)-module \(L\) across the defect by tensoring over \(B\).

terms.label: Conditional expectation
terms.definition:
**Definition (conditional expectation).** For a polynomial observable \(f(x,y)\), average over \(y\) at fixed \(x\) in the normalized Gaussian law,
\[
\mathcal E(f)(x)=\frac{1}{Z_y(x)}\int_{\mathbb R} f(x,y)e^{-S(x,y)/\hbar}\,dy .
\]
Multiplying this function by \(Z_y(x)\) and integrating over \(x\) recovers the original integral with insertion \(f\). From the completed square, \(y\) at fixed \(x\) has mean \(-cx/b\) and variance \(\hbar/b\). Writing \(\langle f\rangle_x=\mathcal E(f)(x)\) gives
\[
\langle y\rangle_x=-\frac cbx,
\qquad
\langle y^2\rangle_x=\frac{c^2}{b^2}x^2+\frac{\hbar}{b}.
\tag{1.2}
\]
{#eq-gaussian-moments}
The second term in \(\langle y^2\rangle_x\) is the conditional variance. At \(x=0\) the mean displacement of the hidden oscillator is zero, yet a detector sensitive to its squared displacement reads \(\hbar/b\) on average.

terms.label: Tensor product over the sector algebra
terms.definition:
A fibre functor to ordinary vector spaces would preserve the unit and fusion up to coherent isomorphisms and so would face this obstruction. At a junction there is more to record than the line \(X\) itself. A sector \(j\) can enter the line and a sector \(i\) can leave it. Use separate commuting actions to select these two labels, a left action for \(i\) and a right action for \(j\). A space with the two actions is called a *bimodule*. For fixed labels the junction space is
\[
V_X(i,j)=\operatorname{Hom}(i,X\boxtimes j)
\]
where a vector is a map from the outgoing simple \(i\) into \(X\boxtimes j\). Let \(A=\mathbb C^3\), with \(e_s\) the coordinate idempotent for sector \(s\). For \(v\in V_X(i,j)\) we have \(e_i v=v\) and \(v e_j=v\). Every other coordinate idempotent on the respective side kills \(v\). These two actions make \(V_X=\bigoplus_{i,j}V_X(i,j)\) an \(A\)-bimodule. For a pair \(v\otimes w\) in the ordinary tensor product \(V_X\otimes V_Y\), select the same intermediate sector on the right of \(v\) and the left of \(w\). The resulting projector is
\[
v\otimes w\longmapsto\sum_i ve_i\otimes e_iw .
\]
In \(V_X\otimes_A V_Y\) the balancing relation is \(ve_s\otimes w=v\otimes e_s w\). If \(v\) has right label \(s\) and \(w\) has a different left label, this relation sets \(v\otimes w\) to zero. On a pair with matching labels the projector is the identity. Such a pair consists of maps \(v:i\to X\boxtimes s\) and \(w:s\to Y\boxtimes j\). Their composite \((\mathrm{id}_X\boxtimes w)\circ v\) maps \(i\) into \(X\boxtimes(Y\boxtimes j)\). In the semisimple Ising category, the space of maps \(s\to Y\boxtimes j\) is the multiplicity space of the simple summand \(s\) in \(Y\boxtimes j\). Decomposing into these summands identifies the direct sum over \(s\) of the matching tensor products with the whole space of maps \(i\to X\boxtimes(Y\boxtimes j)\) by composition. Postcompose with the inverse associator \(\alpha_{X,Y,j}^{-1}\) to obtain a map into \((X\boxtimes Y)\boxtimes j\). Summing over the two external labels \(i,j\) now gives \(V_X\otimes_A V_Y\simeq V_{X\boxtimes Y}\).

For \(X=1,\psi,\sigma\) the junction spaces have dimensions \(3,3,4\), respectively. A spin line accepts one junction for input \(1\), one for \(\psi\) and two for \(\sigma\). Two spin lines have sixteen unrestricted pairs. The matching tensor product keeps six, since the two possible fused lines are \(1,\psi\), each with three junctions. Thus a change in what one tensors accounts for the failure of the scalar dimension test.

In the weak Hopf algebra reconstructed from these three endomorphism blocks, \(\Delta(1)\) acts by the matching projector. The algebra has dimension \(3^2+3^2+4^2=34\), and its tensor unit carries all three sector labels. Fusion determines these dimensions. Specifying which continuation represents an oriented half-exchange also requires the marked braiding. [The Ising half-turn](12-chiral-quantum-groups.md#ch12-ising-half-turn)
