terms.label: Charge measured by a current contour
terms.definition:
The double pole of two currents measures \(k=\kappa\). To read a charge, keep this nonzero numerical level fixed and prepare the endpoint of a rank-one Wilson ray of charge \(a\) in Gaussian abelian Chern–Simons theory. The source couples to the integral of the gauge one-form along the ray oriented into the half-space. Take the endpoint at \(z=0\), use a ray vertical near the boundary current tests and surround it by a positively oriented contour. The contraction of the source with a current gives \(a\,dz/z\). Its residue after weighting by \(z^n\) is \(a\) for \(n=0\) and zero otherwise. Thus only the zero mode of the vacuum action shifts.

For the vertical ray the cohomology on finite sums of angular weights is the charged Fock module
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \mathcal F_a=\mathbb C[p_1,p_2,\ldots]|a\rangle,\qquad J_0=a,\\
 J_{-n}=p_n,\qquad J_n=kn\partial_{p_n}\quad(n>0).
 \end{gathered}
\]
The vector \(|a\rangle\) has no oscillator excitations. Excite the second harmonic once to prepare \(p_2|a\rangle\). The unweighted contour acts by \(J_0\), so it sends this state to \(a\,p_2|a\rangle\). Its charge eigenvalue is the same \(a\) as on \(|a\rangle\). Weighting the contour by \(z^2\) applies \(J_2\) instead. It removes the excitation and gives \(2k|a\rangle\). The coefficient \(2k\) thus measures the oscillator response at the fixed level \(k\).

The double-pole relation is the same in every charge sector. The unweighted contour distinguishes their charges. The endpoint identification on the sector of finite angular weights is Theorem 2.2 of [Chern–Simons observables, charged endpoints and chiral fusion](12-chiral-quantum-groups.md#ref-ch12-cq10).

terms.label: Normal link complex
terms.definition:
**Definition (normal link complex).** For \(n\) distinct labelled points write \(j:\operatorname{Conf}_n(\mathbb C)\hookrightarrow\mathbb C^n\). Let \(L\) be a finite-rank complex local system in degree zero, that is, a family of vector spaces with invertible parallel transport along paths. At a boundary point \(x\), a transverse slice fixes the locations of the clusters and varies the differences inside them. The **normal link complex** \(K_x\) is the cochain complex, considered up to maps inducing cohomology isomorphisms, of the separated part of a sufficiently small transverse neighbourhood with coefficients in \(L\). Its cohomology comprises closed cochains modulo exact ones. In sheaf notation,
\[
 K_x=(Rj_*L)_x
     \simeq\bigl(\operatorname{Cone}(j_!L\longrightarrow Rj_*L)\bigr)_x .
\]
Here \(Rj_*L\) takes sections and their higher cohomology on the part of each neighbourhood lying in the open. Its stalk is obtained by shrinking the neighbourhood to \(x\). Extension by zero \(j_!L\) has zero stalk there. The cone measures the difference of these two extensions, so its stalk at \(x\) is \(K_x\). Complexes use cohomological degrees. A shift \([r]\) moves degree \(a\) to \(a-r\). [Complexes, shifts and homotopies](05-bar-and-coherence.md#cohomology-and-parameters)

terms.label: Attaching map
terms.definition:
A local collision presents the same question before any trace is taken. Knowing the complex of fields away from the collision and the vector space at the collision still leaves the map that continues a field between them. For constructible complexes that datum can be written explicitly. Let \(i:\{x\}\hookrightarrow X\) be a closed stratum and \(j:U=X\setminus\{x\}\hookrightarrow X\) its open complement. Given a constructible complex \(L\) on \(U\) and a complex \(V\) at \(x\), an attaching morphism \(\alpha:V\to i^*Rj_*L\) determines the glued complex by the homotopy pullback
\[
Rj_*L\mathop{\times}^{h}_{i_*i^*Rj_*L} i_*V .
\]
Restriction to \(U\) recovers \(L\), and restriction to the point recovers \(V\). The first projection of the pullback induces precisely \(\alpha\) on that stalk. For the four charge-one rays at level two, take the clean continuation of the separated coefficient over proper collisions. At the deepest collision the degree-two link \(H^2(i^*Rj_*L)\) has dimension two. In the family of perverse quotients by a supported line, the image of the attaching map recovers that line. Its image distinguishes perverse extensions whose stalk and costalk dimensions all agree. For identical rays fix the coordinate frames and the positive half-exchange \(+i\). The permutation action on the link in degree two splits as the trivial character plus the sign character. Exactly their two lines in the projective family admit this equivariance. Ordinary inverse image from the coarse unordered space would require every stabilizer to act trivially on each stalk. Within this family that selects the quotient by the trivial line, the pullback of the downstairs middle extension. A physical collision still has to supply that descent condition or determine the attaching map by a different operation. [The four-point attachment](#atlas-c-cl-05)

terms.label: Consecutive cut
terms.definition:
**Definition (consecutive cut).** For \(0<p<n\), the cut after the \(p\)-th input separates the blocks \(\{1,\ldots,p\}\) and \(\{p+1,\ldots,n\}\). Every point in the first block must be distinct from every point in the second. Thus its open set is
\[
U_{p,n-p}=X^n\setminus\bigcup_{i\le p<j}\Delta_{ij}.
\tag{4.9}
\]
Collisions within either block are allowed. These are the opens used by the consecutive-cut tensor product in Chapter 5.

terms.label: Spencer complex
terms.definition:
The **Spencer complex** adjoins an exterior tangent vector \(e_i\) of degree \(-1\) at each label. Its differential contracts tangent factors with the covariant derivatives, which on the block coefficient are \(\nabla_B=\partial_{z_B}+T_B\). Denote by \(K(I)\) the total complex including the word differential. A surjection \(\alpha:I\twoheadrightarrow J\) gives a map \(K(J)\to K(I)\). It inserts the supported coefficient on the repeated labels and sends
\[
 e_j\longmapsto\sum_{\alpha(i)=j}e_i .
\]
For example repeating a block \(13\) sends its tangent to \(e_1+e_3\), the derivative for moving both labels together. Ordering the quotient labels by their largest preimages determines which adjacent exchanges to apply **inside each word factor**. Taking a maximum in two stages agrees with taking it once. Unitarity and Yang–Baxter identify different presentations of the same order change. The exchange hexagon and the re-rooting identity for the full principal part make these transitions chain maps. Concatenation of two words, followed by localization at all differences between their blocks, gives an associative external multiplication compatible with the support maps. The empty set carries its own scalar \(R\).

terms.label: Supported action of a bulk insertion
terms.definition:
Put the bulk support \(U\subset V\times(a,b)\) above the boundary profile, so that \(\varepsilon<a<b\). To act with a bulk observable \(f\) supported in \(U\), lift the boundary input \(v\) into the collar, multiply by the extension of \(f\), and project the product back to the boundary. This gives
\[
\beta_{U;V}(f)(v)=p^q\bigl(\operatorname{ext}_U(f)\, i^q(v)\bigr).
\]
The middle product is the factorization product after extension by zero. Its two factors have disjoint normal supports, which removes cross terms in the Batalin–Vilkovisky differential there. Both outside maps commute with the differentials. Thus \(\beta_{U;V}\) maps the bulk complex into the complex of continuous boundary endomorphisms, with differential \(D\mapsto dD-(-1)^{|D|}Dd\).

terms.label: Pointed Heisenberg roof
terms.definition: A roof consists of a degreewise surjective state quasi-isomorphism \(p:P\to B\), an admissible state quasi-isomorphism \(i:H\to W\), and a vertex map \(c:P\to\operatorname{Com}(W)\). The actor resolution \(P\) can be unbounded. Admissibility on the boundary requires a bounded-below direct-sum energy grading on \(W\) preserved by \(i,d\), with \(E(a_{(n)}b)=E(a)+E(b)-n-1\) on homogeneous products and locally nilpotent \(i(J)_{(0)}\). The commutant consists of states killed by all nonnegative modes of \(i(J)\). The two commuting images give \(a(x\otimes h)=c(x)_{(-1)}i(h)\). Inverting \(i\) and \(p\otimes1\) gives the value \(i^{-1}a(p\otimes1)^{-1}\) of \(q_B\) on this roof. On \(1\otimes h\) the map \(a\) restricts precisely to \(i\). This supplies the unit path and explains why a change of resolution must respect both legs.

terms.label: Factorized common domain
terms.definition:
**Definition (factorized common domain).** Expand the rational shape coefficients at \(s=0\). A row of the resulting array has fixed \(p\)-exponent, and a column has fixed \(s\)-exponent. In this common space of arrays put
\[
L_D^{\mathrm{fac}}(T)=L_D(T)\cap N_1(T)=L_R(T)\cap N_1(T).
\]
Degree by degree, for each outer exponent \(j\), its \(s^j\)-coefficient belongs to \(T_{12}((p))\otimes M^{(j)}\) for some finite-dimensional graded subspace \(M^{(j)}\subset M_3\). The subspace may grow with \(j\), but it works for the entire inner \(p\)-series at that outer coefficient. This condition makes the intersection a dg \(Y_D\)-module and gives actual maps
\[
L_R(T)\longleftarrow L_D^{\mathrm{fac}}(T)\longrightarrow N_1(T).
\]
For example, the inverse separation of lines 1 and 3 is \(ps/(1+s)\), and that of lines 2 and 3 is \(ps\). A cross term of kernel order \(h\) first reaches column \(h\). Only finitely many such terms act on any prescribed column of a series bounded below in \(s\). The \(12\) kernel can run through all inner orders there because it fixes \(M_3\). The construction preserves quasi-isomorphisms in each input. The outgoing action and factorwise incoming actions preserve it; a general commuting endomorphism of the joint input need not preserve finite spectator support. [The factorized common domain](#atlas-c-horizontal-factorized-common-domain).

terms.label: Upward-proper support
terms.definition: **Definition (upward-proper support).** On each compact set of external parameters, after an external cutoff equal to one nearby, the closure of the joint coefficient support lies in one compact subset of \(M^{I_x}\times\overline M^{I_p}\), where \(I_x,I_p\) label the internal variables. Thus the \(p\)-heights share a lower bound and all complex coordinates have bounded support. Above one upper collar height for this compact set, the current is independent of each such \(p\)-height and has no differential in that height. A bounded family on a fixed compact shares the carrier, the collar height and a finite distribution-order bound after truncating the collars. Particle number is finite, and these operations are defined over \(\mathbb C[\hbar]\).

terms.label: Graph domain for Virasoro sewing
terms.definition:
Take the binary field with input labels \(a,b\) and retain its positive-momentum section, meromorphic germ and vacuum component together (zero when absent). Let \(R_{a,b}\) be the closure of these output tuples in \(\mathscr P_G\times\mathscr M\times G^{\prime}_b\), with the induced topology. At a second positive vertex, the two inner momenta \(p,q\) can vary independently. To form a vacuum coefficient one must multiply two sections at the *same* momentum \(p=q\). For ground packets the value on the diagonal is the pointwise product. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds its \(L^1\) norm by the two \(L^2\) norms. The vacuum functional must still pair against an \(L^2\) packet in the surviving momentum, so we need an \(L^2\) bound on the product itself. One uniform bound and one square-integral bound suffice. At a fixed inner position \(\zeta\), choose \(r<-\log|\zeta|\). Require that the positive section of \(x\) belong to the Banach space

\[
X_r=\{f:e^{rE(p)}f(p)\in C_0([0,\infty);\mathcal F)\cap
                         L^2(d\nu;\mathcal F)\},\qquad
\|f\|_{X_r}=\|e^{rE}f\|_\infty+\|e^{rE}f\|_2 .
\]

**Definition (received positive section).** The domain \(D_r(R_{a,b})\) consists of pairs \((x,f)\in R_{a,b}\times X_r\) for which \(f\) equals the positive section of \(x\). Give it the subspace topology of this product. Thus convergence controls the marked output as well as both positive norms. The measure has full support and \(f\) is continuous, so its values at each momentum are specified. This graph is complete. At the fixed position \(\zeta\), finite preparations are dense in it. For example, let \(h_*=(c-1)/24\), choose a compact ground-energy band in \((h_*,h_*+1)\) avoiding integers, and take a nonzero continuous bump \(f(p)\) supported inside it. The pure ground packet \(f(p)\Omega_p\) with its other marks zero belongs to the graph. For a single original binary preparation at a fixed position the ground coefficient is locally holomorphic along the connected positive momentum axis. The bump vanishes on an open interval outside its support. Analytic continuation would force the ground coefficient to vanish throughout the axis, including where the bump is nonzero.

terms.label: Mehler collar
terms.definition:
The same scalar action on a cylinder of real length \(t\) gives a two-dimensional oscillator of frequency \(n\) and mass \(n^{-2}\) in each complex coordinate. Subtract its ground energy \(n\) before removing the cutoff. The ground-state transform of its heat kernel has mean \(q^n Z_n\) and variance \(n(1-q^{2n})\), where \(q=e^{-t}\). Thus for independent unit-variance circular Gaussians \(\xi_n\),

\[
(P_qG)(Z)=\mathbb E_\xi G\!\left(
  (q^n Z_n+\sqrt{n(1-q^{2n})}\,\xi_n)_{n\ge1}\right),
 \qquad 0<q\le1 .
\]

This is the Mehler semigroup for the independent complex oscillators. At zero length \(P_1\) is the identity. Every \(P_q\) fixes the constant function. In two successive collars the mean becomes \((qs)^n Z_n\) and the independent noises have total variance \(n(1-q^{2n})+q^{2n}n(1-s^{2n})=n(1-(qs)^{2n})\). Thus \(P_qP_s=P_{qs}\). On the holomorphic subspace it is \(q^{L_0}\), with \(L_0=\sum_{n\ge1} nZ_n\partial_{Z_n}\) on polynomials. On \(Z^{\boldsymbol m}\) the generator \(L_0\) has eigenvalue \(e=\sum_n n m_n\), the dimensionless oscillator grade. The collar \(P_q\) multiplies this monomial by \(q^e\). The amplitude with one cylinder inserted is \(\langle F,P_qG\rangle\).

terms.label: Harmonic disk state
terms.definition: To prepare an excited disk, multiply its ground amplitude by a holomorphic polynomial in finitely many \(Z_n\). Completing these polynomials in \(L^2(\mu)\) gives the disk Hilbert space. For the [level-one current](03-local-fields.md#heisenberg-current), the \(n\)th creation mode acts on Fock polynomials by multiplication by \(p_n\), and its adjoint acts by \(n\partial_{p_n}\). The substitution \(V:p_n\mapsto Z_n\) is unitary because on both sides the distinct occupation monomials are orthogonal and \(\|Z^{\boldsymbol m}\|^2=\prod_n n^{m_n}m_n!\). A norm-one amplitude \(F\) therefore gives a probability law \(|F|^2d\mu\) on the harmonic fillings.
terms.source_paragraph: To prepare an excited disk, multiply its ground amplitude by a holomorphic polynomial in finitely many \(Z_n\). Completing these polynomials in \(L^2(\mu)\) gives the disk Hilbert space. For the [level-one current](03-local-fields.md#heisenberg-current), the \(n\)th creation mode acts on Fock polynomials by multiplication by \(p_n\), and its adjoint acts by \(n\partial_{p_n}\). The substitution \(V:p_n\mapsto Z_n\) is unitary because on both sides the distinct occupation monomials are orthogonal and \(\|Z^{\boldsymbol m}\|^2=\prod_n n^{m_n}m_n!\). A norm-one amplitude \(F\) therefore gives a probability law \(|F|^2d\mu\) on the harmonic fillings.

terms.label: Multipoint mode
terms.definition:
**Definition (multipoint mode).** At precision \(d\ge1\), put \(R_d=\mathbb C[\hbar]/(\hbar^d)\) and \(V_d=U/\hbar^dU\), with \(U\) the divided creation algebra. An \(n\)-point mode \([f;a_1,\ldots,a_n]\) has a multiplier \(f\) regular on configurations of distinct nonzero positions and a state \(a_i\in V_d\) at each position. Integration by parts imposes \(\partial_{z_i}+T_i=0\), where \(T_i\) translates the \(i\)-th state. Concatenation multiplies the multipliers. For \(w=[f(x,y);a,b]\), let \(\mathcal S(t)\) be the rational field exchange on \(V_d\otimes_{R_d}V_d\). Its inputs can be any divided states, including translates. Write \(\mathcal S(t)(b\otimes a)=\sum_
u h_
u(t)b_
u\otimes a_
u\). Applying the state exchange and then interchanging the two positions gives
\[
 \sigma w=\sum_
u [f(y,x)\,h_
u(x-y);b_
u,a_
u].
\]
Put \(x=y+u\) at the collision. The one-point mode \(ho w\) at \(y\) takes the \(u^{-1}\) coefficient of \(f(y+u,y)Y(a,u)b\). Impose \(w-\sigma w=ho w\). In a longer word impose this relation at each adjacent pair, keeping the other positions and their poles in the multiplier. Write \(M_d\) for this mode algebra. The empty word is its multiplicative unit \(1\). A separate generator is the occupied point with state \(\mathbf1\) and multiplier \(z^{-1}\), denoted \(\mathsf v=[z^{-1};\mathbf1]\). The normalized algebra is \( ar M_d=M_d/(\mathsf v-1)\), the quotient by the generated two-sided ideal.

terms.label: Cauchy lift of a matrix current
terms.definition:
**Definition (Cauchy lift).** Let \(e_{ij}=\ell_{ij}^{[0]}\) be the matrix-current states. For a Laurent multiplier \(f\), start with \([f;e_{ij}]\). For the term with \(r\) ordered currents, multiply their matrix entries along the chain of indices from \(i\) to \(j\), summing the internal indices, and use the multiplier \(f(z_1)/\prod_{a=1}^{r-1}(z_a-z_{a+1})\) with coefficient \((-\hbar)^{r-1}\). Only \(r\le d\) remains at precision \(d\). In particular the first creation correction is

\[
-\hbar\sum_a [f(x)/(x-y);e_{ia},e_{aj}] .
\]

terms.label: Weak Hopf algebra
terms.definition:
Writing \(V_a\) for the underlying vector space of \(F(L_a)\), reconstruction gives a finite weak Hopf algebra
\[
H=\bigoplus_{a\in I}\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V_a).
\]
The coproduct can be written using the tensor comparison \(J\). Let \(\pi\) project the ordinary tensor onto the relative tensor over \(B\), and let
\[
\iota(v\otimes_Bw)=\sum_i ve_i\otimes e_iw.
\]
Put \(m=J\pi\) and \(s=\iota J^{-1}\). If \(h_M\) denotes the natural action of \(h\) on \(F(M)\), then
\[
\Delta(h)_{M,N}=s_{M,N}h_{M\boxtimes N}m_{M,N},
\qquad
\varepsilon(h)=\lambda\!\left(h_{\mathbf1}\sum_i e_i\right),
\quad\lambda(e_i)=1.
\]
Here \(m s=1\) on the fused coefficient, whereas \(s m\) projects onto matching labels in the ordinary tensor product. Thus \((s h m)(s h' m)=s h h' m\). The associator pentagon gives coassociativity by identifying the two triple splittings. The unit and counit satisfy the weak Hopf identities: the coproduct is coassociative and multiplicative, but \(\Delta(1)\) need not be \(1\otimes1\), and the scalar counit need not be multiplicative. The tensor of representations is
\[
\Delta(1)(V\otimes W),
\qquad
\Delta(1)=\sum_{i\in I}\rho_i\otimes\ell_i,
\]
where \(\rho_i,\ell_i\) are right and left actions of the idempotent \(e_i\in B\). This projection is exactly intermediate-label matching. The reconstruction preserves the ribbon structure and the finite pairing tensor. [GR7](#ref-ch13-gr7)

terms.label: Flux cocycle of a particle junction
terms.definition:
What happens if one inserts the flux twice? Write \(\mathfrak l=\mathfrak g/\mathbb C1\), and lift each polynomial Weyl symbol to its representative with zero constant term. The constant part of the commutator of two lifts is a scalar two-cocycle \(\omega\) on \(\mathfrak l\). Its class acts on the two-sided interval by cap product. Its square vanishes in algebraic cohomology at every numerical \(\hbar\ne0\), even though its four-input representative is nonzero. For example,
\[
 (\omega\wedge\omega)(x,y,x^3,y^3)=3\hbar^4 .
\]
In the Moyal formula the constant coefficient of \([x^d,y^d]\) for odd \(d\) is \(c_d=2d!(\hbar/2)^d\); mixed degrees contribute no constant. The displayed value is \(2c_1c_3\).

terms.label: Finite root jet
terms.definition: **Definition (finite root jet).** An element of \(W_m\) is an \(R\)-linear functional on \(A_m\) which kills every homogeneous root degree above some finite bound. In charge one \(J_i(f)=\partial_x^i f(0)\). In charge two write \(J_0^2(h)=h(0,0)\). Its transpose under the merge acts on \(f\otimes g\) by \(J_0^2(f*g)\). On \(x*1_1,\ 1_1*x,\ 1_1*1_1\) it gives \(\hbar,-\hbar,2\), respectively.

terms.label: Translated Weil test
terms.definition: **Definition (translated Weil test).** Put \(a_j=2^{-20-j}\), \(j\ge1\), and let \(b\) be the density of the infinite convolution of the uniform probability measures on \([-a_j,a_j]\). Normalize \(\phi(x)=e^xb(x)/\|e^{(\cdot)}b\|_2\). For \(n\ge2\) use the two translates \(g_n=\phi+R_{\log n}\phi\) and denote their Weil reading by \(E_n=Q(g_n)\).

terms.label: Retained kernel
terms.definition:
**Definition (retained kernel).** Let \(V=M_3^0\), the ghost-free current states. In the completed ghost algebra \(\mathcal G\), let \(\widehat I_L\) be the closed left ideal generated by modes with index at least \(L\) and put \(F_L=\mathcal G/\widehat I_L\). A degree-\(n\) retained kernel assigns to each algebraic \(w\in V\) a compatible family
\[
T_L(w)\in(V\otimes F_L^n)((u)).
\]
These \(R_3\)-linear families form the retained kernel space \(\mathcal E^n_{\rm ret}\) for \(n\ge0\); put \(\mathcal E^n_{\rm ret}=0\) for \(n<0\). Their Laurent lower bound may depend on \(L\) and \(w\). The combined current–ghost differential \(\mathscr D\) on these kernels squares to zero. The ghost differential itself is evaluated at a larger cutoff before projection; the individual \(F_L\) are not thereby dg quotient algebras. A retained cochain has an additional state input: in degree \(j\) it belongs to
\[
\mathcal Q^{\mathrm{ret},j}
=\prod_{p\ge0}\operatorname{Hom}_{R_3}
\bigl(M_3^p,\mathcal E^{p+j}_{\rm ret}\bigr),
\qquad
\delta\Psi=\mathscr D\Psi-(-1)^j\Psi d_M.
\]
There are two independent choices here. The inserted state \(x\in M_3^p\) chooses the kernel \(\Psi(x)\), of ghost degree \(p+j\). On a current \(w\in V\), its value at cutoff \(L\) has coefficients in \(V\otimes F_L^{p+j}\). A functional on its ghosts can then read a coefficient. The term \(-(-1)^j\Psi d_M\) in the Hom differential records the differential of the inserted state.

terms.label: rooted input of an operation
terms.definition: To compare an endpoint operation before and after the exchange, first insert a current state \(w\), then pair the output ghosts with a chosen functional. An output proportional to a single ghost has zero vacuum coefficient, yet its coefficient against the dual of that ghost can be nonzero. We call \(w\) the **rooted input** because it stays in the second position.

An output proportional to a single ghost has zero vacuum coefficient, yet its coefficient against the dual of that ghost can be nonzero. terms.label: Poisson transvectant
terms.definition:
Let \(V\) be a nonzero finite-dimensional symplectic vector space over \(k\), \(A=k[V]\) its polynomial functions, and \(\pi\) the Poisson bivector, with \(\pi(dx,dy)=1\) on a Darboux plane. In linear coordinates with components \(\pi^{ij}\), put \(\Pi=\sum_{i,j}\pi^{ij}\partial_i\otimes\partial_j\), and let \(\mu\) multiply the two polynomial factors. The \(m\)-th Poisson transvectant is \(B_m(f,g)=\mu\Pi^m(f\otimes g)\) for \(m\ge1\). In particular \(B_1=\{-,-\}\). On a single plane,
\[
 B_m(f,g)=\sum_{i=0}^m(-1)^i\binom mi
 (\partial_x^{m-i}\partial_y^i f)(\partial_x^i\partial_y^{m-i}g).
\]

terms.label: formal local scalar bracket
terms.definition: A formal local scalar bracket takes two elements of \(A[[t]]\) to an element of \(A[[t]]\). It is alternating and \(k[[t]]\)-bilinear. On polynomial inputs, the coefficient of each power of \(t\) must be a bidifferential operator of finite order with polynomial coefficients. Impose covariance under translations and the full linear symplectic group of \(V\). Fix the classical bracket at \(t=0\) to be \(B_1\), and require \([p,q]_t=\pi(p,q)\) exactly on all linear Hamiltonians \(p,q\in V^*\).

terms.label: exchange at energy two
terms.definition: **Definition (exchange at energy two).** On the span of \(a,b\) let \(Sa=b\) and \(Sb=a\). The matrix of \(S\) in this orthonormal basis is real and symmetric. Its eigenvectors \(u_+,u_-\) have eigenvalues \(+1,-1\), respectively. Thus a measurement of this self-adjoint observable reads the sign with certainty on either preparation. On a general unit state \(\alpha a+\beta b\) its expectation is \(2\operatorname{Re}(\bar\alpha\beta)\).

terms.label: cubic current observable
terms.definition:
**Definition (cubic current observable).** The sum of the splitting and joining operations over ordered pairs of positive indices defines the operator
\[
W=\frac12\sum_{i,j\ge1}\bigl(J_{-i}J_{-j}J_{i+j}+J_{-i-j}J_iJ_j\bigr).
\]
{#eq-cubic-observable}
On a monomial of energy \(e\), a split requires an occupied harmonic \(i+j\) and a join requires the two quanta \(i,j\). Either can occur only when \(i+j\le e\), so the sum is finite on polynomials. Its adjoint pairs preserve each finite-dimensional energy space, where their sum \(W_e\) is self-adjoint. At energy two only \(i=j=1\) occurs, and \(W_2=O/2=S\). On the Hilbert completion the self-adjoint direct sum has domain \(\{F=\sum_e F_e:\sum_e\|W_eF_e\|^2<\infty\}\) and value \(WF=\sum_eW_eF_e\), where \(F_e\) is the orthogonal energy-\(e\) component.

terms.label: density wave
terms.definition:
The simplest symmetric polynomials are the power sums
\[
p_n(x)=x_1^n+\cdots+x_N^n=\sum_{a=1}^Ne^{2\pi iny_a/L},\qquad n\ge1 .
\]
Thus \(p_n(x)\) is a Fourier coefficient of the density of particles, and multiplying a wavefunction by it adds momentum \(2\pi\hbar n/L\). A polynomial \(F(p_1,p_2,\ldots)\) in the Fock space of the current now defines a state \(F(p(x))\,\psi_0(x)\) of the fermions. Multiplication by \(p_n\), which creates a quantum of the \(n\)th harmonic, becomes multiplication by a density wave.

terms.label: Schur polynomial
terms.definition:
For a partition \(\lambda=(\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_N\ge0)\) the quotient
\[
s_\lambda(x)=\frac{\det\bigl(x_a^{\lambda_b+N-b}\bigr)_{a,b=1}^N}{\Delta_N(x)}
\]
is a symmetric polynomial, the Schur polynomial of \(\lambda\).
terms.source_paragraph: *Proof.* For a partition \(\lambda=(\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_N\ge0)\) the quotient

terms.label: heterodyne reading
terms.definition: An ideal heterodyne receiver measures both quadratures of one oscillator mode. In each run it returns a complex number \(\alpha\), with probability density \(\langle\alpha|\rho|\alpha\rangle/\pi\), where \(|\alpha\rangle\) is the coherent state of amplitude \(\alpha\). For the \(n\)th harmonic put \(Z_n=\sqrt n\,\bar\alpha_n\). The vacuum then gives \(Z_n\) the Gaussian law of variance \(n\), and a state with amplitude \(F\) gives the law \(|F(Z)|^2\,d\mu\).

terms.label: matrix factorization
terms.definition: **Definition (matrix factorization).** Over \(R=k[[x]]\), a matrix factorization of \(W\in R\) is a \(\mathbb Z/2\)-graded finite free module \(P\) with an odd operator \(Q\) satisfying \(Q^2=W\,1_P\). Its boundary operators form the algebra \(\operatorname{End}_R(P)\) with differential \(d=[Q,-]\).

terms.label: residue trace
terms.definition: **Definition (residue trace).** Fix the coordinate volume \(dx\) at an isolated one-variable critical point. The sphere functional on \(\operatorname{Jac}(W)\) is \(\tau_W(h)=\operatorname{Res}_0 h(x)\,dx/W'(x)\), the coefficient of \(x^{-1}\) in \(h/W'\). It gives the bulk pairing \((h,g)\mapsto\tau_W(hg)\).

terms.label: gradient screening
terms.definition: **Definition (gradient screening).** For \(f_i=\partial_i W\), the screening differential \(D\) is the residue of the normally ordered current \(\sum_i:f_i(\gamma)c^i:\). Its self-product is regular, since none of its constituents contract with one another. Thus \(D^2=0\). As a zero mode it commutes with translation \(T\) and differentiates every vertex product. At weight zero \(Db_i=f_i,\ D\gamma_i=0\), precisely the bulk Koszul complex. A regular gradient sequence gives the Jacobi ring in degree zero. At positive weight two contractions can contribute to a single residue. [Malikov and Schechtman, chiral Koszul complexes](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1406.0284) · [Dedushenko, Landau–Ginzburg chiral algebras](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1511.04372)

theorems.title: Lemma (occupation inner product)
theorems.statement_excerpt:
**Lemma (occupation inner product).** With vacuum norm one and \(J_n\) adjoint to \(J_{-n}\), there is a unique positive Hermitian inner product on the polynomials. We take it conjugate-linear in the first entry. Different occupation monomials are orthogonal, and
\[
\bigl\|p_1^{m_1}p_2^{m_2}\bigr\|^2=m_1!\,2^{m_2}\,m_2!.
\]
{#eq-two-harmonic-norms}

theorems.title: Example (A cubic and a quartic boundary)
theorems.statement_excerpt:
Start with upper right entry \(x\) and lower left entry \(x^{r-1}\). Displace the upper entry to \(x+t\). Can a change of the lower entry keep the same potential through order \(N\) in \(t\)? Set \(t^{N+1}=0\), so that terms through order \(N\) can be compared exactly. A lower entry \(b(x,t)\) would have to satisfy \((x+t)b(x,t)=x^r\). Substitution of \(x=-t\) in a formal \(x\)-series is legitimate since \(t\) is nilpotent. It forces \(t^r=0\). Conversely the finite geometric sum gives
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 b_r(x,t)=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}(-t)^j x^{r-1-j},\\
 (x+t)b_r(x,t)=x^r-(-t)^r .
 \end{gathered}
\]
Thus the displacement is possible through order \(N\) precisely for \(N<r\). Retaining terms through \(t^3\) distinguishes the two boundaries. Before truncation the cubic square acquires \(+t^3 I\), while the quartic square first changes by \(-t^4 I\).

How can a third insertion detect the difference when two agree? Let \(E_{ij}\) denote the elementary matrices in the even, odd basis. The linear term of the displaced matrix is \(t\psi\) with \(\psi=E_{12}-x^{r-2}E_{21}\). The differential on boundary operators is \(dB=QB-(-1)^{|B|}BQ\), where \(|B|\) is the parity. Its square is \(Q^2B-BQ^2=0\). A closed operator satisfies \(dB=0\), and two closed operators give the same protected class if their difference is exact, that is, of the form \(dH\). For \(f,g,u,v\in\mathbb C[[x]]\), direct multiplication gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 d\,\operatorname{diag}(f,g)&=x(g-f)\psi,\\
 d(uE_{12}+vE_{21})&=(xv+x^{r-1}u)I .
 \end{aligned}
\]
The even cycles are multiples of \(I\), the odd cycles multiples of \(\psi\), and the exact multiples in either parity have coefficient in \((x)\). The classes \([I],[\psi]\) therefore form a basis over \(\mathbb C\). Since \(\psi^2=-x^{r-2}I\) is exact, the two potentials give the same ordinary multiplication.

For an odd change \(\alpha\) of \(Q\), the change in its square is \(d\alpha+\alpha^2\). Our choice of lower entry cancelled each coefficient up to the first scalar unit, which survives in cohomology. In the coordinates of this displacement, three copies of \([\psi]\) have higher product \(+[I]\) for the cubic. For the quartic it takes four copies to give \(-[I]\). [The higher products in the one-variable model](19-interacting-theories.md#ch19-boundary-potential)

theorems.title: Proposition (the centre acting on modules)
theorems.statement_excerpt: **Proposition (the centre acting on modules).** Let \(A\) be a unital associative algebra over a field. An \(A\)-linear operator \(T_M\) on every left \(A\)-module \(M\), satisfying \(fT_M=T_Nf\) for every module map \(f:M\to N\), is multiplication by a unique element of the centre \(Z(A)=\{z\in A:za=az\text{ for all }a\in A\}\).

theorems.title: Open problem (bulk reconstruction)
theorems.statement_excerpt: **Open problem (bulk reconstruction).** Fix the class of coherent actions on boundary observables, including their restrictions to separated points and their behavior at collisions. Does a geometric centre represent those actions, and under what hypotheses do the supported bulk insertions induce an equivalence from bulk observables to this centre that preserves factorization? [Bulk actions and the universal centre](17-holographic-reconstruction.md#bulk-action-and-centre)

theorems.title: Proposition (The algebra of strict Lie couplings)
theorems.statement_excerpt: Define the universal enveloping algebra \(U(\mathfrak g)\) by taking words in \(\mathfrak g\), with concatenation as product and the empty word as unit, and imposing linearity in each letter and \(xy-yx=[x,y]\). Unital algebra maps \(U(\mathfrak g)\to B\) are in natural bijection with the degree-one solutions of the Maurer–Cartan equation in \(C\otimes B\).

theorems.title: Proposition (diagonal action)
theorems.statement_excerpt:
**Proposition (diagonal action).** Let \(H\) be a unital associative algebra and let \(\Delta:H\to H\otimes H\) be linear. Formula (2.1) defines a unital action on the tensor product of every pair of left \(H\)-modules precisely when
\[
\Delta(hh')=\Delta(h)\Delta(h'),\qquad
\Delta(1_H)=1_H\otimes1_H.
\tag{2.2}
\]

theorems.title: Ising fusion over the algebra of sectors
theorems.statement_excerpt:
In the Ising conformal field theory at central charge \(1/2\), the three simple sectors are the vacuum \(1\), a fermion \(\psi\), and the spin sector \(\sigma\). A simple sector has no proper nonzero subobject. Fusion, denoted \(\boxtimes\), combines two sectors and can split into a direct sum of possible channels. The fusion rules include
\[
\begin{aligned}
\psi\boxtimes\psi&=1,\\
\psi\boxtimes\sigma&=\sigma,\\
\sigma\boxtimes\sigma&=1\oplus\psi .
\end{aligned}
\]
Suppose a faithful additive assignment to finite-dimensional complex vector spaces were to send the vacuum to \(\mathbb C\) and fusion to ordinary tensor product. The first rule would make the fermion space one-dimensional. The last would then require the spin space to have integer dimension \(d\) with \(d^2=2\).

A fibre functor to ordinary vector spaces would preserve the unit and fusion up to coherent isomorphisms and so would face this obstruction. At a junction there is more to record than the line \(X\) itself. A sector \(j\) can enter the line and a sector \(i\) can leave it. Use separate commuting actions to select these two labels, a left action for \(i\) and a right action for \(j\). A space with the two actions is called a *bimodule*. For fixed labels the junction space is
\[
V_X(i,j)=\operatorname{Hom}(i,X\boxtimes j)
\]
where a vector is a map from the outgoing simple \(i\) into \(X\boxtimes j\). Let \(A=\mathbb C^3\), with \(e_s\) the coordinate idempotent for sector \(s\). For \(v\in V_X(i,j)\) we have \(e_i v=v\) and \(v e_j=v\). Every other coordinate idempotent on the respective side kills \(v\). These two actions make \(V_X=\bigoplus_{i,j}V_X(i,j)\) an \(A\)-bimodule. For a pair \(v\otimes w\) in the ordinary tensor product \(V_X\otimes V_Y\), select the same intermediate sector on the right of \(v\) and the left of \(w\). The resulting projector is
\[
v\otimes w\longmapsto\sum_i ve_i\otimes e_iw .
\]
In \(V_X\otimes_A V_Y\) the balancing relation is \(ve_s\otimes w=v\otimes e_s w\). If \(v\) has right label \(s\) and \(w\) has a different left label, this relation sets \(v\otimes w\) to zero. On a pair with matching labels the projector is the identity. Such a pair consists of maps \(v:i\to X\boxtimes s\) and \(w:s\to Y\boxtimes j\). Their composite \((\mathrm{id}_X\boxtimes w)\circ v\) maps \(i\) into \(X\boxtimes(Y\boxtimes j)\). In the semisimple Ising category, the space of maps \(s\to Y\boxtimes j\) is the multiplicity space of the simple summand \(s\) in \(Y\boxtimes j\). Decomposing into these summands identifies the direct sum over \(s\) of the matching tensor products with the whole space of maps \(i\to X\boxtimes(Y\boxtimes j)\) by composition. Postcompose with the inverse associator \(\alpha_{X,Y,j}^{-1}\) to obtain a map into \((X\boxtimes Y)\boxtimes j\). Summing over the two external labels \(i,j\) now gives \(V_X\otimes_A V_Y\simeq V_{X\boxtimes Y}\).

For \(X=1,\psi,\sigma\) the junction spaces have dimensions \(3,3,4\), respectively. A spin line accepts one junction for input \(1\), one for \(\psi\) and two for \(\sigma\). Two spin lines have sixteen unrestricted pairs. The matching tensor product keeps six, since the two possible fused lines are \(1,\psi\), each with three junctions. Thus a change in what one tensors accounts for the failure of the scalar dimension test.

In the weak Hopf algebra reconstructed from these three endomorphism blocks, \(\Delta(1)\) acts by the matching projector. The algebra has dimension \(3^2+3^2+4^2=34\), and its tensor unit carries all three sector labels. Fusion determines these dimensions. Specifying which continuation represents an oriented half-exchange also requires the marked braiding. [The Ising half-turn](12-chiral-quantum-groups.md#ch12-ising-half-turn)

theorems.title: Lemma (An order-two distribution on the diagonal)
theorems.statement_excerpt:
For a formal distribution \(D(z,w)\) killed by \(t^2\), put
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 A(w)=\operatorname{Res}_z D\,dz,\\
 B(w)=\operatorname{Res}_z tD\,dz .
 \end{gathered}
\]
Then \(D=A(w)\delta(z,w)+B(w)\partial_w\delta(z,w)\).

theorems.title: Proposition (free-current contraction)
theorems.statement_excerpt:
**Proposition (free-current contraction).** In the neutral polynomial representation at level \(\kappa\), the product with \(J(w)\) acting first is
\[
\begin{aligned}
J(z)J(w)
&=:J(z)J(w):+[J_+(z),J(w)]\\
&=:J(z)J(w):+
\kappa\sum_{n\geq1}n z^{-n-1}w^{n-1}\\
&=:J(z)J(w):+
\kappa\,\iota_{z,w}\frac1{(z-w)^2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.10}
\]

theorems.title: Example (the normal-product associator)
theorems.statement_excerpt:
**Example (the normal-product associator).** The normally ordered square prepares \(p_1^2\). To compute \((j_{(-1)}j)_{(-1)}j\), take the constant term of \(:J(z)^2:\) on \(j=p_1\). The power from two modes \(J_m,J_n\) is \(z^{-m-n-2}\), so \(m+n=-2\). The two creation indices must both be \(-1\) when both are negative. If one index is positive, only \(J_1\) can remove the quantum in \(p_1\), and both orders \((-3,1),(1,-3)\) occur. The zero mode vanishes. Moving \(J_1\) to the right gives \(J_1j=\kappa\mathbf1\) in each mixed term. Reversing the *grouping* instead applies the constant mode of \(J(z)\), multiplication by \(p_1\), to \(p_1^2\). The two answers are
\[
(j_{(-1)}j)_{(-1)}j=p_1^3+2\kappa p_3,\qquad
j_{(-1)}(j_{(-1)}j)=p_1^3.
\]
The associator is \(2\kappa J_{-3}\mathbf1=\kappa T^2j\). At every nonzero level it distinguishes the field product from ordinary polynomial multiplication.

theorems.title: Proposition (ternary diagonal operations)
theorems.statement_excerpt: **Proposition (ternary diagonal operations).** For ordinary right differential modules with the fully localized source and unshifted target of (4.3), the linear spans of composites through \(12|3\) and \(1|23\) have zero intersection. Consequently a strictly associative binary operation in these spaces has zero triple products.

theorems.title: Theorem: classical factorization and chiral algebras
theorems.statement_excerpt: **Theorem: classical factorization and chiral algebras.** The above category of unital factorization algebras is equivalent to the category of unital Beilinson–Drinfeld chiral algebras on \(X\). The factorization sheaves acquire a canonical differential-module structure, and the corresponding right differential module is \(\omega_X\otimes B_{\{1\}}\).

theorems.title: Theorem (simultaneous cluster twists)
theorems.statement_excerpt:
**Theorem (simultaneous cluster twists).** Suppose the coincident points at \(x\) form nontrivial blocks \(S_1,\ldots,S_b\). A positive full twist of a block rotates all its points once around their common centre while leaving the other blocks apart. Let \(C_i\) be its action on a common fibre \(E\), using local base paths. Then
\[
 K_x\not\simeq0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \bigcap_{i=1}^b\ker(C_i-1)^{\dim E}\ne0 .
\]
Conjugating the local representation does not change the criterion. The twists commute with each other and with the angular monodromies in this local product, even when the angular monodromies fail to commute among themselves.

theorems.title: A projective line of four-ray attachments
theorems.statement_excerpt:
The two-dimensional space \(H^2K\) is large enough to contain many different image lines of an attaching map. Which lines can actually occur? Work on the labelled transverse slice \(\mathbb C^3\), with \(i\) the inclusion of its origin. Use middle-perversity support and cosupport conditions. The resulting category of perverse sheaves is abelian, so one can form a quotient by a subobject supported at the origin. A degree-zero local system on the smooth open threefold is placed in ordinary degree \(-3\), by the shift \([3]\).

Write \(V=H^2K\) and \(V'=H^3K\). In this example extension by zero \(P_!=j_!L[3]\) is perverse. Its intermediate extension \(j_{!*}L[3]\) has no nonzero subobject or quotient supported on the boundary. The part lost in passing from the former to the latter is the point-supported \(i_*V\), giving the exact sequence
\[
 0\longrightarrow i_*V\longrightarrow P_!
 \longrightarrow j_{!*}L[3]\longrightarrow0 .
\]
For each line \(W\subset V\), form the quotient \(P_W=P_!/(i_*W)\) in the perverse category. Its ordinary stalk is \(i^*P_W\simeq W[1]\). The costalk \(i^!P_W\) measures local cohomology supported at the origin. Since \(i^!P_!\simeq K[2]\), the costalk sequence gives \(H^0 i^!P_W=V/W\) and \(H^1 i^!P_W=V'\), with all other groups zero.

Thus the stalk has one class in degree \(-1\), and the costalk has ranks one and two in degrees zero and one, for every line. The quotients also agree off the origin. The attaching map \(i^*P_W\to K[3]\) on \(H^{-1}\) has image the particular line \(W\subset V\). Indeed its image is the kernel of the boundary map \(V\to H^0i^!P_W=V/W\). An isomorphism of two such sheaves acts on the separated rank-one local system by a scalar and, by naturality of \(j_!\), must carry one embedded kernel in \(P_!\) to the other. A scalar fixes each line. Hence distinct \(W\)'s give distinct isomorphism classes parametrized by \(\mathbb P(V)\cong\mathbb P^1\). This calculation concerns extensions on the fixed labelled slice. A comparison with an oriented Hall coefficient must identify the attaching morphisms and respect the other collision maps.

theorems.title: Two parameters with the same tangent class
theorems.statement_excerpt:
Take \(S=\mathbb Q[u,v]/(u^3,v^3)\) with maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m=(u,v)\). The parameters \(r=u\) and \(r'=u+v^2\) have the same nonzero class in \(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\). Both fourth powers vanish, but their cubes are
\[
 r^3=0,\qquad (r')^3=3u^2v^2\ne0 .
\]
Indeed the monomials \(u^a v^b\) with \(0\le a,b<3\) form a basis of \(S\). The cubic boundary is flat at \(r\) and has scalar obstruction \(3u^2v^2\,1\) at \(r'\). The quartic boundary is flat at both marked parameters.

theorems.title: A primitive generator tests the augmentation
theorems.statement_excerpt: Let \(C=k1\oplus kc\) with zero differential and \(c\) primitive of degree \(-1\). Then \(X=uc\) has degree zero and \(d_\Omega X=0\). Thus \(\Omega C=k[X]\), with augmentation \(X\mapsto0\). Take \(A=k\) with its identity augmentation. Evaluation at \(X=1\) gives a unital dg algebra map. A reduced twisting cochain takes \(c\) into \(\ker(k\to k)=0\), so its map must send \(X\) to zero. This is the unique augmentation-preserving evaluation. On the coalgebra side \(Bk=k\), and the corresponding map is the counit of \(C\).

theorems.title: Theorem: connected consecutive-cut duality
theorems.statement_excerpt: **Theorem: connected consecutive-cut duality.** In \(\mathcal W_X\), bar and cobar for consecutive-cut convolution are inverse equivalences between connected augmented coherent associative algebras and connected counital coaugmented coherent coassociative coalgebras. The equivalence includes their full mapping spaces. It requires no cohomological boundedness or finite-dimensionality of coefficients.

theorems.title: Support theorem
theorems.statement_excerpt:
**Support theorem.** Consecutive-cut duality restricts to an equivalence between connected factorizing coalgebras and connected algebras whose positive-arity coefficients vanish on every cut open. For a connected factorizing coalgebra \(C\) and \(n\ge1\),
\[
\overline{\Omega C}_n\simeq R\Gamma_{Z_n}(C_n)[-1].
\]

*Proof.* Start with two letters. The one-block cobar term is shifted by \([-1]\) and the two-block term by \([-2]\). Factorization identifies their arrow before shifts with \(C_2\to Rj_*j^*C_2\). Its fibre shifted by \([-1]\) is the binary reduced cobar coefficient. With \(n\) letters choose a subset of the \(n-1\) gaps. If it has \(r-1\) members it cuts out \(r\) blocks. The cobar shift is \([-r]\), one lower than the shift \([-(r-1)]\) in the localization cube. On the intersection of these cut opens the iterated coproduct identifies the coefficient with the external product of the \(r\) block coefficients. Coassociativity makes these identifications commute with adding a cut. The total fibre of the localization cube computes sections supported off the union of the opens. Comparing the shifts at each vertex gives the cobar coefficient an additional shift \([-1]\).

Conversely, assume the positive algebra coefficients vanish on the cut opens. Fix one cut and restrict the bar to its open. A bar factor straddling the cut has zero coefficient, since that factor itself admits the cut. Every surviving term therefore has a separator at the chosen gap. A multiplication face that removes this separator has zero target. Each remaining face, including a higher multiplication face, acts wholly to its left or wholly to its right. Splitting at the separator identifies the two complexes in the definition above. ∎

theorems.title: Theorem (the algebraic collision integral)
theorems.statement_excerpt: **Theorem (the algebraic collision integral).** Form \(G_U(V)\) by taking an algebraic direct sum over chains of surjections, placing a chain of length \(p\) in simplicial degree \(-p\), with the usual alternating face maps on the \(K(I)\). Shuffling two chains and concatenating their coefficient words makes \(G_U(V)\) a unital dg algebra over \(R\). Its degree-zero cohomology is the intrinsic all-arity mode algebra \(\mathsf M_U(V)\).

theorems.title: Conditional unit theorem for inflated coefficients
theorems.statement_excerpt:
**Conditional unit theorem for inflated coefficients.** For every simple \(\mathfrak g\) and every \(k\in\mathbb C\), under the smooth realization hypotheses of (6.1), the actual unit
\[
T\xrightarrow{\eta_T}\Psi\Phi T
\]
is an equivalence for every ordinary unbounded \(H\)-complex inflated along \(q\), and therefore for every inflated \(R\)-complex. This holds with arbitrary algebraic internal support or without an internal grading.

theorems.title: Finite descent theorem
theorems.statement_excerpt: **Finite descent theorem.** Under the split-extension, K-flatness and tensor-vanishing hypotheses above, the actual unit is invertible on every \(L\in D(B)\) if it is invertible on every unrestricted inflated \(R\)-complex.

theorems.title: Theorem (sharp tensor exponent)
theorems.statement_excerpt:
**Theorem (sharp tensor exponent).** For the positive-weight ideal \(I\) at \(s\in\mathbb C\setminus\mathbb Q\), the first vanishing derived tensor power over \(R=U(\mathfrak g)\) is one more than the number \(D\) of positive roots. More precisely,
\[
 I^{\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}D}\not\simeq0,\qquad
 I^{\otimes_R^{\mathbf L}(D+1)}\simeq0
 \quad\text{in }D(R\otimes R^{\mathrm{op}}).
\]
This is an assertion about the bimodule with its two multiplication actions. It holds in the algebraic internal grading and after forgetting that grading. [The sharp tensor exponent](#atlas-c-ur-10).

theorems.title: Conditional full-unit theorem
theorems.statement_excerpt:
**Conditional full-unit theorem.** At nonrational shifted level \(s\), in every finite-dimensional simple complex type, assume the smooth realization (6.1) with its specified right action, common Taylor cutoffs and enhanced homogeneous tensor–Hom comparison. For every ordinary unbounded \(B\)-complex \(L\) the original unit is an equivalence
\[
 \eta_L:L\xrightarrow{\sim}\Psi\Phi L .
\]
This holds for the ungraded adjunction and for algebraic internal grading with arbitrary support. Algebraically, (6.4) has at most \(D+1\) inflated \(R\)-complex factors. If \(R\otimes_B^{\mathbf L}L=0\), (6.5) first gives \(T_1(L)\simeq L\). The same base change now vanishes on \(T_1(L)\), and induction gives \(L\simeq T_{D+1}(L)=0\). Thus scalar extension detects zero objects. The affine assertion uses the additional fact that \(\eta\) is invertible on every inflated factor. Its naturality squares and the finite triangles then give \(\eta_L\). [The full unit and its hypotheses](#atlas-c-ur-05).

theorems.title: Theorem (complementary-level pairing)
theorems.statement_excerpt: **Theorem (complementary-level pairing).** Over \(\mathbb C\), let \(\gamma\) represent the Tate determinant extension in the lift given by normal ordering at \(\mathfrak p\), with its canonical splitting on \(\mathfrak p\). For smooth modules \(M,N\) with cocycles \(\eta,\eta'\), the normally ordered semi-infinite operator \(Q\) for the diagonal action on \(M\otimes N\) satisfies \(Q^2=1_{M\otimes N}\otimes\operatorname{cl}_{\mathfrak p}(\eta+\eta'+\gamma)\) on \(M\otimes N\otimes\mathcal F_{\mathfrak p}\). For the abelian pair \(x,y\) with lattice \(\mathbb Cx\), let \(x,y\) act by \(\partial_u,u\) on \(\mathbb C[u]\) and take \(N\) trivial. With matter coefficient \(1\), the vacuum satisfies \(Q^2\Omega=0\), while the state with one antighost satisfies \(Q^2(b_y\Omega)=c_x\Omega\ne0\). Here \(b_y\) creates \(y\) and \(c_x\) wedges by \(x^*\). Take the second central extension to be the negative of the sum of the first and the determinant extension. In compatible lifts its cocycle is \(\eta'=-\eta-\gamma\), so \(Q^2=0\). The resulting semi-infinite cohomology pairing identifies \(\mathcal S_{-\eta-\gamma}\) with the categorical dual of \(\mathcal S_\eta\). The complementary raw affine level is \(-\ell_0-2h^\vee\), and the complementary Virasoro charge is \(26-c\). For Witt modes the nonnegative lattice \(P_0\) gives the categorical pairing. Changing the normal ordering from modes \(r\ge-1\) to \(r\ge0\) adds \(d\lambda\) to the determinant cocycle, where \(\lambda(L_n)=\delta_{n,0}\). With the first lift fixed, the second uses \(L_0-1\) at the same charge.

theorems.title: Lemma (one real-root reflection)
theorems.statement_excerpt: **Lemma (one real-root reflection).** Let \(\beta\) be a positive real affine root and let \(\widehat\rho\) pair to one with the affine simple coroots. If the complex highest weight \(\xi\) satisfies \(\langle\xi+\widehat\rho,\beta^\vee\rangle=q\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\), there is an injection of ordinary affine Verma modules \(M(\xi-q\beta)\hookrightarrow M(\xi)\).

theorems.title: Smooth completeness from a common current tail
theorems.statement_excerpt:
Every cohomology module of the input \(X\) in (6.13) has trivial positive-current action. An infinite family representing a nonzero class in \(H^0R\Gamma_{\mathfrak a}(iX)_0\) has no primitive with a common torsion exponent. There is a different way to recover a smooth complex from its underlying module complex. Its truncations discard successively fewer low cohomological degrees. To compare their inverse limit with the original complex, first forget smoothness and then take derived smooth vectors. Put
\[
\mathfrak n=t\mathfrak{sl}_2[t],\qquad
\mathfrak n_L=t^L\mathfrak{sl}_2[t],\qquad
F:D(\mathcal S)\longrightarrow D(\mathfrak M),
\quad G=R\operatorname{sm},
\]
where \(\mathcal S\) is the smooth positive-current module category and \(\mathfrak M\) is the category of all positive-current modules. The functor \(F\) forgets smoothness. Its right adjoint derives the smooth-vector functor \(\operatorname{sm}(M)=\bigcup_{L\ge1}M^{\mathfrak n_L}\). Use algebraic integer-energy gradings, with currents lowering energy and maps preserving it. Products are taken energy by energy before the outer algebraic direct sum.

Suppose one tail annihilates all sufficiently low cohomology: there are \(L\ge1\) and an integer \(b\) such that
\[
\mathfrak n_LH^q(X)=0\qquad(q\le b).
\]
Then the actual unit is an equivalence,
\[
X\xrightarrow{\sim}GF(X)
\simeq\operatorname{holim}_n\tau^{\ge-n}X,
\]
with no bound on higher cohomology, multiplicities or energy support. For every smooth derived source \(Y\), the original map
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{D(\mathcal S)}(Y,X)
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Hom}_{D(\mathfrak M)}(FY,FX)
\]
is an isomorphism, including all shifts. [Common-tail completeness](#atlas-c-induction-common-tail-completeness).
