introduction:
If you could measure a quantum field only at its boundary, could you tell which state had been prepared in the interior? A preparation is a repeatable way of setting up the field. Its state tells you the probabilities of the readings you can obtain. To distinguish two preparations, you need a measurement for which those probabilities differ.

Consider a wave on a circle. Its first harmonic oscillates once around the circle, its second harmonic twice. Take a free massless field for which energy per excitation is proportional to frequency. A single excitation is called a quantum. One quantum of the second harmonic then has the same energy as two quanta of the first. Call the state with two quanta in the first harmonic \(a\), and the state with one in the second \(b\). Leave all other harmonics unexcited.

Both alternatives can be present in a single quantum state. Prepare the sum \((a+b)/\sqrt{2}\) or the difference \((a-b)/\sqrt{2}\). Count the quanta in each harmonic. With either preparation, half the time you find two in the first and none in the second, and half the time you find none in the first and one in the second. The probabilities are the squared magnitudes of the two coefficients. Counting loses their relative sign. Even an arbitrary measurement on the first harmonic alone misses it. To compare the two alternatives, the measurement would have to connect a state with zero quanta in the second harmonic to one with a single quantum there.

A joint measurement can do just that. Let \(S\) turn two quanta of the first harmonic into one of the second, and conversely, so that \(Sa=b\) and \(Sb=a\). A state which an observable multiplies by a number gives that number whenever the observable is measured. Here the exchange leaves the sum fixed and multiplies the difference by \(-1\). Measuring it gives \(+1\) with certainty in the first preparation and \(-1\) with certainty in the second.

How could a field produce this exchange? A probe placed just inside the boundary of a free field in three dimensions can remove an excitation from a chosen boundary harmonic. An insertion on the boundary can add one. Remove a quantum from the second harmonic and add two to the first, or carry out the reverse process. Set the fluctuation scale \(\hbar\) and bulk coefficient \(\kappa\) so that the boundary current has level \(\hbar\kappa=1\). Write \(p_j\) for creation of a quantum of harmonic \(j\). A unit probe acts on these polynomials by \(\beta(u_j)=\partial_{p_j}\), and the current mode which removes a quantum is \(J_j=j\beta(u_j)\). Use twice the strength of a single second-harmonic probe in the first process. In the reverse process use two unit first-harmonic probes, one after the other at separate heights. The sum of these field operations acts as \(2S\) on our two states. Its outcomes are \(+2\) on the sum and \(-2\) on the difference. [The two paths through the vacuum](#fig-energy-two-exchange)

To test this calculation independently, fill a disk with a fluctuating harmonic field. Its value at an interior point is the average of its values on a small circle centred there. With finitely many harmonics, the field energy fixes their vacuum probability density. Adding further harmonics preserves this marginal law. Write \(Z_1,Z_2\) for the complex amplitudes of the first two harmonics. In the vacuum they are independent centred complex Gaussians with mean-square magnitudes \(1,2\). Call their joint law \(\mu\). Preparing the sum or the difference weights this law by \(\left|(Z_1^2\pm Z_2)/2\right|^2\). In each pattern, compare the phase of the second harmonic with twice the phase of the first, weighting their alignment by the strengths of both waves. The reading \(C=2\operatorname{Re}(Z_1^2\overline{Z_2})\) fluctuates. Its average is \(+2\) in the sum preparation and \(-2\) in the difference preparation, just as the interior probes predict. [How the two measurements are calculated](#ch11-relative-phase)

The instrument in this example measures wave patterns extending around a whole circle. Keep all the harmonics and take a circle of radius \(0<r<1\) in the unit disk. At each point multiply the squared gradient of the harmonic field by its outward radial derivative. Take \(r^3/8\) times the angular average of this product. Its mean is \(+r^4\) in the sum preparation and \(-r^4\) in the difference. These means approach the two exchange eigenvalues. In either preparation, as in the vacuum, the probability that one reading lies in any fixed bounded interval tends to zero as \(r\uparrow1\). An observer can also place two probes in small regions of the boundary and vary the distance between them. The joint signal may grow as the regions approach. One would like to replace the pair by fields at a single point and calculate their contributions to the signal. In the *chiral* theories studied here, these contributions depend holomorphically on position. Away from a collision they are locally power series in one complex coordinate. At a collision they can have poles. [The fluctuations of the circle average](#eq-cubic-disk-escape) · [Fields at separated and coincident points](#fields-and-modes)

Place a third probe on the curve. We can bring the first two fields together and then bring in the third, or begin with the last two. Each calculation starts near a different collision. To compare the two products, we must put them on a common domain. Here the fields form a complex. They are arranged in degrees, with a differential \(d\) that takes one degree to the next and satisfies \(d^2=0\). The two products are related by an operation called a *homotopy*. On inputs killed by \(d\), applying \(d\) to its output gives the difference of the two products. With four fields this correction itself enters a product. The five ways of placing parentheses give two routes between the extreme parenthesizations, and a further homotopy relates the routes. These are comparisons for an ordered multiplication. The ordinary chiral Lie bracket of Beilinson and Drinfeld takes the two fields to a field supported where the points meet. It obeys skew-symmetry and the Jacobi identity. To compare the two ordered products one must also give their multiplication and the homotopy between its bracketings. [The bracket at a collision](#lie-and-operator-product) · [The ordered products](#ch05-one-differential-encodes-all-associativity-homotopies)

The field operation and the disk integral give the same two means by different calculations. To build further experiments, an instrument must first admit a consistent coupling to the field. The Lie brackets give one such condition, the action on two probes gives a coproduct, and the exchange of marked probes tests more than the action on either one. In a one-variable boundary model even the order of the first obstructed coupling distinguishes \(x^3\) from \(x^4\). The marked cubic has a three-input product equal to the unit. For the quartic the three-input product vanishes and four inputs give minus the unit. [Which couplings a probe admits](#opening-consistent-couplings) · [Combining and exchanging two probes](#opening-composition-of-probes) · [The two boundary deformations](#opening-boundary-interactions)

An *associative chiral algebra up to homotopy* keeps these comparisons for arbitrarily many fields. Its coefficients are complexes on the spaces of marked points on the curve. They carry rules for differentiating in the positions and for restricting the complexes as positions coincide. Fix a word giving the order of multiplication. Its *bar construction* lists the inputs before multiplication and has a differential combining consecutive inputs by the operations of the algebra. A cut divides the word into two consecutive blocks. Wherever every point of one block is distinct from every point of the other, cutting identifies the bar coefficient with the tensor product of the two block coefficients. The full collision space has a chart for each ordering. There the factorization rule applies to every ordered division of the labels.

In the word construction, one can reverse the passage from products to cuts. Keep the full coefficient complexes, including their restrictions at collisions, and their compatible cut maps. Require the empty coefficient to be the scalars, with its specified inclusion and projection. On a smooth separated complex algebraic curve of finite type the inverse construction, called *cobar*, recovers the algebra with its homotopies and its full spaces of maps. A word on \(n\) labels has at most \(n\) nonempty blocks, so the construction terminates at each number of labels even for infinite-dimensional fields. The algebra coefficient on three labels can have support only where both cuts fail. This is precisely where the first and third points agree, even if the middle point sits elsewhere. [Recovering the algebra from ordered cuts](#ch05-ordered-cuts-give-a-finite-geometric-bar-construction)

At the chain level this inverse uses just the operations needed to merge or split a word. In a cochain complex the differential raises degree. A quasi-isomorphism preserves its cohomology in every degree. The bar construction takes a coherent associative algebra to a coalgebra in which iterating nonempty cuts on a fixed word eventually gives zero, called a conilpotent coalgebra. A twisting cochain is the degree-one comparison from a coalgebra to an algebra whose differential compensates for applying the coproduct and then the product. It supplies the maps between bar and cobar and explains why the comparison can recover the homotopies as well as the cohomology. [The maps between bar and cobar](#ch05-cobar-reverses-the-construction)

Why do these operations need an ordered space of collisions? There is another construction on a curve, the ordinary *chiral bracket*. Its coefficients carry the differential operators in each point position, which makes them differential modules. It takes a polar field on the complement of a diagonal to a field supported on the diagonal. Keeping the unshifted target and allowing all poles, the spans of the two possible three-field composites intersect only in zero. An ordinary strictly associative product on that carrier would therefore have all triple products zero. In the ordinary vertex-algebra description locality allows products in reversed order to be compared after a power of the separation clears the pole. The ordinary chiral operation satisfies a Jacobi identity. Its singular coefficients can be read together by weighting its Laurent series with an exponential and taking the residue, the lambda bracket. On a smooth curve its unital algebras are equivalent to classical factorization algebras, sheaves on powers of the curve with compatible vacuum and collision maps. The associated Ran space remembers the finite set occupied by the points. On the ordered configuration space the consecutive cut keeps the order in which those points are used. [The three residues and the classical construction](#ch04-three-residues)

What can a fourth-order operation tell us that the binary products have left undecided? The universal principal chiral algebra called \(W_4\) has currents of spins two, three and four. Its vacuum is a representation of these currents. The algebra of maps from the vacuum to itself, computed with a resolution, records its self-extensions and their higher products. At the exceptional shifted level \(-3/2\), symmetry makes the ternary operations vanish in a compatible choice of representatives. One coefficient of a quartic operation remains. The same binary algebra and the same two first-order maps on its cohomology are compatible with every value of that coefficient. Calculation on the original vacuum resolution gives zero. Here the algebra of derived vacuum endomorphisms is formal, meaning that its cohomology with its ordinary multiplication recovers it up to equivalence. [The exceptional four-input calculation](#ch12-exceptional-w4-fibres-and-the-algebra-of-extensions)

At a generic level the vacuum self-extension algebra of this theory has dimension eight. At the four shifted levels \(3/2,-3/2,2/3,-2/3\) its dimension is twelve. Two local torsion summands, each killed by the first power of the level parameter, each contribute a pair of classes to the exceptional fibre. That is why specializing the field equations before taking cohomology matters. Even the product of two classes which survive specialization can vanish there. In an elementary triple Massey product, two adjacent products are exact. Combining their chosen primitives with the two outer inputs produces a closed field.

Knowing where a collision can contribute still leaves the question of how a field reaches that locus. Move four identical charged lines around one another in a free theory, each with charge one at level two. On a fixed labelled slice, a whole projective line of attachments at the fourfold collision gives the same measured full turns and the same numbers of local cohomology classes in each degree, both at the collision and with support there. Fix the coordinate frames and require the positive half-exchange to multiply by \(+i\). Precisely two of those choices respect permutation symmetry. Requiring the coefficient to come from the ordinary space that forgets the labels selects one. In an irregular collision even a loop can miss how a solution grows as it approaches the singularity. In an explicit three-point family, transport around the singularity is the identity for every value of an extension parameter. Comparing the solutions coming from two different directions detects exactly when the extension splits. [What survives a collision](#ch04-irregular-collision)

There is a general way to test whether a collision has nearby classes available to attach. Take a local system of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces on configurations of distinct labelled points in the complex plane. Rotate the points of one colliding cluster once counterclockwise about their common centre while the other clusters stay apart. On a common fibre \(E\), transport around the loop for cluster \(i\) gives a linear map \(C_i\). Write \(I\) for the identity on \(E\). The normal link complex measures what approaches the collision in the transverse directions. It has nonzero cohomology exactly when there is a nonzero vector \(v\in E\) such that \((C_i-I)^{\dim E}v=0\) for every \(i\). Such a vector is a common generalized fixed vector for the full twists. For a single colliding pair with \(C=-I\) on a one-dimensional fibre, the circle differential is \(C-I=-2I\), so both cohomology groups vanish. When nearby classes do survive, an attaching map specifies which of them extend across the collision. The four charged rays display the difference between the two questions. [The simultaneous full-twist criterion](#ch04-normal-link)

Once the collision maps are given, one can pass from fields depending on positions to operators on states. Integrating a field against a power of its coordinate selects a mode. On an affine line with finitely many punctures we construct an algebraic complex that also admits integrals of several fields together. For flat families with translation, weakly associative fields and compatible invertible Laurent-polynomial exchange, its degree-zero cohomology is the algebra of all these modes. Interchanging two neighbouring fields changes an integral by their collision residue, with the other fields still present. [Integrating fields in several positions](#ch05-rational-exchange-diagram)

There is a precise way to keep all the coefficients the residue can see. Work first to finite order in the normal derivatives at a collision and retain the restriction from each order to the preceding one. This inverse system is a *pro-object*. On the affine line with a chosen coordinate, take symmetric and exterior powers of the principal parts of one Heisenberg current, with zero central contractions in the Cousin differential. The Vandermonde is a product of differences of the auxiliary variables. Transposing multiplication by it identifies the two dual systems and their vacuum maps. Each cut contributes the factors formed from differences across its two blocks. The comparison retains the extension at three positions where the first and third coincide while the second remains elsewhere. Each finite stage, with its bounded state, pole and normal-derivative data, may be specialized in the level. To implement differentiation of an integrated coefficient, the Spencer complex adjoins a tangent variable for each marked point. Its differential applies the position derivative together with field translation. The direction of the dual map has reversed under transposition. To use it as a forward operation on fields one still needs a forward action. [Duality retaining all normal derivatives](#ch13-supported-duality-and-the-direction-of-comparison)

The distinction between single fields and several fields survives integration. In a two-by-two matrix-current example, products of single modes have classical coefficients regular where two points meet. A genuine two-point mode has a pole there. The prescribed single-current operators still give an injective copy of the determinant-one quantum matrix algebra through first order in its deformation parameter. At the next order the same choice would require a particular mixed residue to vanish. At critical level \(-2\), with the two remaining positions fixed at \(1\) and \(2\), its value is \(1/3\). The residue detects the failure in the mode algebra itself. [Which matrix-current relations survive](#ch12-rational-matrix-fields-and-the-full-curved-dual)

On states themselves the comparison goes further. For determinant-one matrix currents of every rank at least two and at any complex level, the formal quantum double is topologically free over the power series in the deformation parameter. Its creation and annihilation halves give its completed tensor decomposition, and its integral fields and their exchange agree on every state with the quantum affine fields. Setting the parameter to zero in the state field algebra recovers the universal affine vertex algebra of trace-free matrices. The current operators used for the multipoint test were the prescribed Cauchy lifts. This explains how the all-state field theorem can coexist with a failed relation in the larger multipoint mode algebra. A completed dual has its own issue. A *contramodule* is a chosen recipient with coherent rules for evaluating the allowed infinite sums of coefficients. A general equivalence for the curved dual requires the corresponding class of equivalences on both module categories. [The two recipients for the matrix currents](#ch12-rational-matrix-fields-and-the-full-curved-dual)

A second calculation retains what a scalar field would discard. A retained kernel keeps the ghost coefficients until they act on a specified state. A rooted operation has one distinguished input on which its coefficients act. Take these inputs in the marked rank-two current theory and work through the square of the quantum parameter, setting its cube to zero. For the rank-two currents away from critical level the cohomology fields are ordinary translated products. The trace sector survives, and the additional degree-three class has zero square and zero derivative. A normalized homotopy compares the two prescribed marked kernels on the full algebraic rooted inputs. At critical level the quadratic invariant of the currents and its derivatives acquire degree-one partners. Their polynomials and exterior products, together with the degree-three ghost and the trace sector, determine the free module of states at that precision. The field and differential on the state complex are constructed at this precision. Explicit singular products in the listed critical generators and an independent physical comparison are further questions. [What changes at critical level](#ch17-native-r3-fields)

Which of these local products could we recover by observing the systems on which the fields act? Two theories built from different lattices in sixteen dimensions have the same rules for combining and exchanging their sectors and the same number of states at each energy. They differ in the field multiplying the inverse separation when two symmetry currents meet. For an ordinary unital chiral algebra on such a curve, we can recover the product from its complete families of representations together with the geometric realization of their vacuum, the state inserted at an otherwise unoccupied mark. The realized two-point coefficient carries arbitrary incoming fields through their collision. Multiply this coefficient by integer powers of the separation and read off the term in the inverse separation, the residue. These readings recover the chiral product. [Recovering a chiral product from the vacuum family](#ch13-the-ordinary-categorical-round-trip)

Combining two systems that share a symmetry raises a further question. How does each symmetry operation act on the pair? A *chiral quantum group* expresses that action in terms of operations on the two systems, consistently with how their local fields multiply and exchange positions. *Holography* asks which experiments in the interior, or bulk, can be recovered from those boundary operations. In gravity the geometry inside can itself fluctuate. A boundary theory would then have to predict how the state is prepared by a particular filling and what happens when two such fillings are joined.

The free current gives a test of what a joint symmetry must preserve. Its level is the coefficient of the double pole in its product with itself. On two independent systems the mixed product has no pole, so adding the currents adds their levels. The resulting map runs from fields at the sum of the levels to fields acting on the pair. This is a *coproduct*. For a class of Hopf algebras with translation and a compatible invertible Laurent-polynomial pairing governing exchange, we construct such maps for all fields. Here the levels are symmetries of the Hopf algebra, and their ordered composition gives the level acting on the pair. The tensor product includes the factor for crossing one incoming field past the other. With that factor, applying the coproduct before or after a field product gives the same answer, and the two ways of applying it to three systems agree. [Fields and their coproduct](#ch12-a-spectral-construction-of-products-and-coproducts)

In a rational theory the same question can have a finite answer. In the Ising theory two spin fields can combine to give the vacuum or the fermion. Joining two such processes requires their intermediate labels to match. Keeping those labels reconstructs a symmetry algebra of dimension \(34\), a *weak Hopf algebra*. Its coproduct sends the identity to the projection onto the matching pairs. On three spins, exchanging the first pair twice and exchanging the last pair twice act differently on the two fusion paths. After their common phase is removed, one operation changes the relative sign of the paths and the other exchanges them. Their products and linear combinations give every two-by-two matrix on this space. [What exchanges of spin fields measure](#ch12-ising-half-turn)

The operation on a pair that interchanges its factors is the braiding, and the change in how a triple is grouped is its associator. In the Ising ribbon category, which also remembers duals and the twist of one strand, linear combinations of ordered products of adjacent double exchanges give all the intertwiners of every tensor power of the spin field. Orientation can be measured by a half-exchange. The ratio of its two labelled eigenvalues is \(i\), and reflection changes that ratio to \(-i\). The matching-sector tensor product retains the intermediate label on which those operators act. In the spectral construction the position-dependent pairing is the spectral form. Compatibility of multiplication with the chiral coproduct is the bialgebra condition for these fields. Producing this structure for an arbitrary associative chiral algebra is open. [The orientation of an exchange](#ch12-ising-half-turn)

Can a whole space of states be recovered after it passes through an interface between two theories? The algebraic operation of *induction* tensors a representation of a line algebra with a module carrying the actions on both sides. Maps out of that module give the return operation. For a simple affine current algebra, take the module generated by a state killed by the positive modes, with the constant modes acting freely on its top. At a nonrational shifted level, suppose the specified line algebra acts on this smooth module from the right, realizes its derived endomorphisms with the corresponding order of composition, and supplies the tensor–Hom adjunction with compatible cutoffs on its resolution. The round trip then recovers every complex of line modules, including unbounded ones. On the current side it recovers exactly the part generated by that module under shifts, extensions, sums and direct summands. The bound in the proof is the number of positive roots of the current symmetry. For the currents of traceless three-by-three matrices three positive-weight factors can survive in the derived tensor over the constant-mode algebra, and a fourth always vanishes. [The interface and its range](#affine-reconstruction-scope)

The raw affine level is the coefficient of the central term in the current commutator. Shifting it by the dual Coxeter number gives the level used in the finite bound. In a smooth affine module every vector is killed by all sufficiently high positive modes. The finite bound is useful because the round-trip comparison is already invertible, under the smooth realization, on unrestricted complexes brought up from the stated quotient, even at critical level. Finite descent extends it from these coefficients when the augmentation is split, the coefficient presentation is K-flat on both sides, and a derived tensor power of the augmentation ideal over the constant-mode algebra vanishes. The tensor and return maps are computed with K-flat and K-injective resolutions. The first preserves acyclicity on tensoring. Maps from an acyclic input into the second form an acyclic complex. A separate completion theorem applies to energy-graded positive currents of traceless two-by-two matrices. If one tail of the positive modes kills all sufficiently low cohomology, passing from smooth modules to all modules and taking derived smooth vectors returns the original complex. If every cohomology vector is also killed by all sufficiently long products of positive currents (joint augmentation torsion), the trivial module and its energy shifts generate this complex. Joint torsion alone permits a tower with nonzero cohomology that these shifts fail to detect. The tower is built from the positive modes of a raising matrix. Every derived map from a shifted trivial module to it vanishes. Under the smooth hypotheses at nonrational shifted level, the image of affine induction is the localizing subcategory generated by the inducing module. The proof does not require the inducing module to be a compact object, one from which mapping commutes with arbitrary direct sums. For a finite-dimensional simple complex Lie algebra, normalize the long roots to have squared length two. At the critical raw level, minus the dual Coxeter number (\(-2\) for \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\)), quadratic currents on the right vacuum give a different tower. Its cohomology is nonzero and jointly torsion, yet every derived map into it from a shift of the inducing module vanishes. It therefore lies outside the subcategory generated by that module. Both vanishing results hold over \(\mathbb C\) in the algebraically energy-graded and the ordinary ungraded smooth derived categories. Inducing the linear tower for \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) gives an object that receives a nonzero degree-zero map from the inducing module shifted to energy \(-2\) at every complex raw level. Whether this induced object belongs to the generated subcategory remains open. At noncritical levels it is also open whether that subcategory contains every smooth complex with jointly torsion cohomology. A physical interface must separately realize the adjunction unit and counit, the two comparison maps for its round trips. [The round trip and the common tail](#ch06-common-tail-completeness) · [The positive-current tower](#ch06-theorem-a-complex-orthogonal-to-all-positive-current-cells) · [The critical affine tower](#ch06-theorem-a-critical-affine-complex-orthogonal-to-the-regular-top)

Joining two line ends tests more than transporting a single representation. In the algebraic particle coupling of a membrane with \(N\geq1\) particles, at nonzero quantum parameter and zero Cherednik deformation parameter, ordinary multiplication returns the whole particle algebra. Its first derived correction vanishes too. In the next homological degree a flux survives. The position and momentum of a particle commute only up to a scalar, and this scalar commutator defines an operation on the complex for joining the two ends. In degree two it maps onto the entire particle algebra and has a right inverse. A physical interval with these ends would have to reproduce that operation. [Flux on a joined pair of line ends](#ch14-what-a-joined-interface-remembers)

Applying the flux operation twice gives a different answer from applying it once. Write \(\hbar\) for the scalar in the particle commutator. The four-input representative of the square of this flux cocycle takes the nonzero value \(3\hbar^4\) on position, momentum and their cubes, but this four-input cocycle represents zero in algebraic cohomology. No primitive depending on a fixed finite order of Taylor derivatives at the marked point can produce that cancellation. The scalar in the position–momentum commutator also prevents a map to scalars preserving multiplication at nonzero \(\hbar\). Keeping that scalar as curvature gives an integral description of the full relative matrix complex for one, two and three particles by a curved cobar construction. It works before division by the parameter, and at zero parameter its derived fibre is formal. Over the field of rational functions of the parameter the comparison extends to every rank, and the fourth multiplication is nonzero from rank three onward. For a stack of surfaces, a separate test on two ordered, separated collars gives opposite derivative contributions when their order is reversed. With two level-one surface collars and the specified incoming magnetic strength, the reading to first order in the five-dimensional loop parameter \(\hbar_{\mathrm b}\) is \(+\hbar_{\mathrm b}/(8\pi^2)\) on the marked current state. The ordered spin-two Miura field gives half its own parameter on that same state, fixing that parameter to \(\hbar_{\mathrm b}/(4\pi^2)\) for these marks. Extending it to coincident surfaces requires a physical fusion law. [Ordered surface probes](#ch14-surface-fusion-and-the-miura-product)

Another defect gives an independent test of which fields lie in the image. A stack of \(N\) D3 branes has gauge-invariant operators whose protected products are confined to one complex line. A separate geometric construction uses the space of length-\(N\) configurations of points, including their infinitesimal collisions, in the complex two-dimensional plane. Restrict its global fields to those generating finite-dimensional spaces under the torus action and set the quantum parameter to one. At every rank the framed relative polynomial gauge complex has cohomology only in degree zero. Its algebra embeds in those global fields as precisely the kernel of a specified odd charge. There is a global field on which that charge gives the nonzero scalar \(N\). Thus the same construction identifies the operators obtained and a field outside their image. [The exact image of the brane fields](#ch14-d3-branes-chiral-operators-and-hilbert-scheme-sections)

On a brane the BRST differential is the square-zero operator implementing the gauge constraint. Its cohomology tests whether a field survives after gauge equivalence is imposed. The D3 example recovers exactly the stated kernel on its protected line. Recovering a bulk action on a family of boundary conditions requires a different test, one which compares how the same operation acts on every member of the family.

There is a second question one can ask of the action on boundary states. Which operations are compatible with every change of boundary condition and every collision of its fields? For ordinary modules, the module-linear operations natural in all modules form the centre of their algebra. On a curve the compatibilities include homotopies. There is a recognition theorem for a test system with two separately multiplying sectors. Its coefficients give each cluster of points one of the two labels. Let the system acting on it be built from clusters labelled by a differential graded chiral algebra on the affine line with a closed unit preserved by the connection. Choose its vacuum operation coherently through all collisions. A *character* here is a map from this system to the two-labelled one that preserves the chosen vacuum up to the specified homotopy. Inserting the target vacuum into an action recovers its character. Multiplying by the character recovers the entire action and its homotopies. Which of these geometric operations can an interior field produce? [Recognition from the vacuum action](#ch07-recognition-on-chevalley-coalgebras)

The acting coefficient system and its coherent map from the local vacuum are called an actor and pointing. The vacuum hypothesis itself can be tested. For a chiral algebra without a unit on the affine line, adjoining one preserves the complete character and action spaces if its marked cohomology class admits a closed horizontal representative. For a commutative differential graded algebra with a compatible connection this recognition holds for every coherent marking. A *homotopy fibre* keeps the actual identification with the marked operation, all choices of that identification and the homotopies among them. For the ordinary derived centre the corresponding complex of operations is given by Hochschild cochains. A proposed chiral centre must represent the geometric action problem on the full family of sources one intends to use. [Which vacuum markings suffice](#ch07-recognition-on-chevalley-coalgebras)

How many choices can a derived space of operations have? Give an exterior algebra \(r\) generators of degree one with zero differential and translation. Its space of maps to any ordinary differential graded vertex algebra is computed by two entries for each nonempty subset of generators, with equations given by translation and the simple-pole product. For two generators there are six entries. For a scalar target the components for general \(r\) have \(r+\binom r2\) independent scalar coordinates and the loops in each component have \(r\) more. A pointed Heisenberg roof represents an operation by first replacing the marked source with an equivalent complex and then mapping into the target, retaining the vacuum identification. Does this describe every genuine pointed action on a nonzero-level current? Over \(\mathbb C\), for one exterior generator of degree one acting on a rank-one current of nonzero level, the answer is yes. The charge and the constant part distinguish the components of the space of actions. When both vanish, scaling the exterior generator connects the action to the projection. Each component has additive fundamental group \(\mathbb C\) and vanishing higher homotopy groups. [The finite exterior calculation](#ch07-finite-exterior-sources) · [The components of the genuine action space](#ch07-theorem-components-of-the-genuine-heisenberg-action-space)

A field in the interior should act consistently on every boundary condition to which it can be brought. We can test such an action on the boundary of the free abelian theory in the opening experiment. Place a probe above a thin layer carrying the boundary current. Multiply it by a boundary input and integrate out the transverse fields. On empty input the chosen probe gives zero. In the presence of a current the two fields can contract. With the normalization of the circle experiment, a probe tuned to one harmonic acts on any polynomial in the modes by differentiating with respect to that harmonic. This is the removal operation that enters the exchange. Write \(p_j\) for the operation of adding one quantum of harmonic \(j\). On its polynomial representatives, a unit probe \(u_j\) acts by \(\beta(u_j)=\partial_{p_j}\), whereas the level-one current mode acts by \(J_j=j\partial_{p_j}\). On the input \(p_2\) the single probe gives \(1\) and \(J_2\) gives \(2\). This is the factor of two used in the first path through the vacuum. [The contraction of the interior probe with a boundary mode](#ch11-relative-phase)

Two interior probes introduce a further comparison. They may first be brought to different heights above the boundary, or moved together until their boundary positions coincide. In a free theory with one real height and one complex boundary coordinate, the first differential of an ordered pole includes a term supported at coincident boundary positions whenever the second probe lies above the first. Differentiating the height step in that term gives a contact exactly where the two heights and the two boundary positions agree. It cancels the differential of the bulk kernel. Dropping it would make the differential fail to square to zero. A third field can also change which products are defined. A series whose successive coefficients involve independent states of that third field is a perfectly good series of three-field states. It cannot be expressed using finitely many states of the third field after the pair has already been completed. For products we must therefore specify a domain common to both orders. In the circle experiment the polynomials in the harmonics give such a domain for adding and removing excitations. [Fields at different heights](#ch09-ordered-poles-and-their-complete-differential)

For rational currents this domain can be computed. With any finite number of radially arranged inputs, the specified smooth affine realization, its full round-trip unit and the cofree and generation hypotheses give an evaluation preserving the outgoing action and the commuting incoming actions. For three poles the rational resolution acts on the intersection of the joint and separately completed coefficient arrays, the factorized common domain. The coordinatewise tensor completion allows a coefficientwise limit even when no finite set of spectator states contains its coefficients. If the third input has finite total cohomology, it also reaches the independently factorized endpoint. Finite dimension in each degree does not suffice. At four poles one can complete two disjoint pairs independently and construct evaluation on their common coefficient arrays using separate resolutions. For three spectator points left free, at positive odd pole bound for pairs of marked points and arbitrary nonnegative bounds at the spectators, the corresponding bounded-pole residue complex in charge \(q\geq2\) has no cohomology below degree \(q\), including where those three points coincide. This still leaves the integral comparison at the collision itself with a separately composed pair of line operators. [The common domain for three poles](#ch08-factorized-common-domain)

With height as well as position there is another domain condition. For finite pole and derivative orders take compatible collision subspaces, the specified height-ordering factors and the common distributional extension of the whole arrangement. The construction requires upward-proper support. On every external compact set, the joint support is compact after adjoining the upper height endpoint for each \(p\)-variable. The complex coordinates stay bounded, the \(p\)-heights have a common lower bound, and above one collar the current is constant in each upper height with no differential in that height. The finite marked Ward calculus is then closed under the full differential, including residues on the coincident loci. The first and successive circuit contacts and their admitted products with spectators have a continuous radial limit in the original relative current complex. Integrating the radial derivative gives a chain homotopy to that limit, also for the computed two-mark contact with the allowed disjoint spectators. On a compact elliptic curve an independent evaluation still has to match the supported contact with its previously fixed lower homotopies. In the free circle experiment the relevant domain and the measurements on it can both be specified directly. [Transport of the supported contacts](#ch09-relative-currents-and-a-radial-homotopy)

How much of a state can these harmonics reveal? At level one, where the first harmonic in the vacuum has variance one, the joint probability law of the complex harmonic amplitudes on a marked disk determines every density matrix in the sector of zero total charge, including statistical mixtures. For finitely many harmonics the disk energy gives their Gaussian vacuum density. Divide the measured joint density by it. The Taylor coefficients of the resulting function give all the matrix elements of the state restricted to those harmonics. Increasing the number of harmonics recovers every matrix element of the full state. [Recovering a state from disk measurements](#ch11-recovering-a-state-from-the-disk)

We can also test which state a particular interior source prepares. Let two lines carrying real charges \(a\) and \(-a\) rise from the points \(r\) and \(0\) of the unit disk, with \(0<r<1\). A contour enclosing both lines sees zero total charge, but the \(n\)th harmonic of the surrounding current reads \(ar^n\). Independently, give the real harmonic disk field a point source at \(r\), with its constant mode fixed. If the field value there is \(\phi(r)\), the source multiplies its probability weight by \(e^{a\phi(r)}\). The disk integral gives the same joint law, shifting the mean of the \(n\)th harmonic to \(ar^n\) and leaving its variance equal to \(n\). A cylinder of length \(-\log q\) damps that harmonic by \(q^n\). The normalized overlap of the prepared state with its propagated state is \(\bigl((1-r^2)/(1-qr^2)\bigr)^{a^2}\) for \(0<q\leq1\). The factor \(r^{-a^2}\) acquired by the two lines cancels from this comparison. [The charged lines and the sourced disk](#ch11-neutral-ray-pair)

In the half-space one can also compare two presentations of the same measurement. Splitting a spatial form into terms with and without the holomorphic differential identifies the compact Gaussian field complexes of the marked free abelian theory at matched levels. This map preserves their differentials, disjoint products and unit. On these complexes a mixed contraction in the projection supplies the supported boundary action that removes a mode. A probabilistic operation appears on the scalar cylinder. Given the boundary harmonics at its first end, the Gaussian kernel at the other end takes a conditional expectation, averaging over the added fluctuations. This Mehler collar propagates the harmonic disk state from the independent point source. The zero harmonic measures the charge of a current module and vanishes on the neutral pair. Dividing the collar matrix element by the squared norm, its zero-length value, gives the normalized state reading and cancels the factors from both ends. [The two marked half-space constructions](#states-lines-and-caps)

What information can such a normalization conceal? Two fillings of a solid torus can agree near a prescribed cut and its outer collars and have the same classical action on each side. Choose a pair of field modes supported in one of the regions where the fillings differ, and integrate them on the same contour with the same measure. For a specified deformation the unnormalized amplitudes have ratio \((64+8i)/65\). Dividing each by its vacuum amplitude removes the phase. Enlarging the finite integral to sample both regions gives ratio one even before this division. [Two fillings with a common measure](#ch11-independent-meridian-measure)

To join two surfaces along a circle, a state prepared on one side must be a permissible input on the other. A *conformal block* assigns amplitudes to the incoming states. Cutting a four-punctured sphere in two different ways gives two expansions of such an amplitude. For the positive principal Virasoro representations at real central charge greater than one, the intermediate state has a continuous momentum as well as discrete energy levels. Assuming the normalized four-point channel changes, their pentagon identity and the two-radius energy estimates, sewing along any finite tree converges uniformly on compact subsets of its strictly separated region in logarithmic sewing coordinates, with every momentum and every energy level retained. On a common domain the change of channel intertwines the two answers. A collision output can nevertheless grow too rapidly to serve as another unrestricted input, even after a cylinder of any fixed finite length. The widths of the intermediate collars decide which successive sewings the theorem permits. [When a sewn state can be used again](#ch10-finite-uncut-sewings)

Under the normalized boundary hypothesis, which fixes both expansions of the original four-point block and their common comparison, one can construct a complete space of admissible inputs inside each of these channel spaces. It is dense there, respects continuous maps of Virasoro representations, and gives the original topologies on the positive and vacuum objects. Vector fields with finite polar parts act by convergent mode sums. For two independently completed pairs, a graph domain controls both the energy norm and the pointwise size of their momentum distributions. There the positive output pairs the two distributions with the kernel, while the resolved vacuum output keeps their common momentum. Two ground-state packets of width \(\varepsilon\) can have fixed individual Hilbert norms and a product whose norm grows as \(\varepsilon^{-1/2}\). An outgoing operation descends to the whole chosen completion only if it annihilates the kernel of preparation and remains continuous for that completion. [What two independent completions can sew](#ch10-two-completed-clusters)

Closing a boundary can hide an entire product. In Hall multiplication one keeps the possible ways of building an object as an extension of two others. The two orders of multiplication keep the same nested subobjects, which proves associativity. On a particular polarized K3 surface, three stable line bundles give a test against nilpotent representations of a doubled directed graph satisfying its quadratic relation. Given a cyclic comparison of their extension complexes preserving the three vertex units, the ordinary Hall algebras generated by the bundles and by the simple vertex representations agree in every charge. This result concerns how objects can be joined. What can a measurement see after their boundary is closed? [Two geometric constructions of Hall multiplication](#ch15-a-faithful-ordinary-comparison-on-a-k3-surface)

There is a local version of Hall multiplication in which one measures derivatives in internal root coordinates. For the one-loop polynomial shuffle algebra, the cobar on finite root jets in charge \(m\) has cohomology only in degree \(m\), where it is the algebra prescribed by the exchange relations in that charge. The contraction preserves finite jet support over the polynomial parameter ring. This is the Hall correspondence on internal degrees of freedom. To turn their multiplication into a collision of fields at different external positions, one must transport the coefficient of the extension correspondence and its orientation root, a square root of the associated determinant line. On a specified product of a Kummer K3 surface and an elliptic curve, the two chosen classes of perfect complexes generate a group of semi-topological components isomorphic to \(\mathbb Z^2\). These components are the connected classes under deformation. On their union the fixed compact orientation root has exactly two isomorphism classes of enhancements compatible with its square and associative on all finite flags. In the compact reduction, rigidification removes a known central stabilizer. The relative moment values still enter the flags. On a compact surface the comparison must also preserve the state pairing and intermediate moment parameters before taking their traces. [What the one-loop Hall calculation computes](#ch15-one-loop-on-finite-root-jets)

A tube in relative curve-counting theory on a compact K3 surface gives an operator on its boundary states. Joining the ends contracts its two indices to a trace. For primitive curve classes the generating series of the normalized traces is minus the reciprocal of the weight-ten Igusa cusp form. Leaving three circles open gives a different measurement. On an elliptic K3 with rational section \(C\) and one point at each boundary, the section contribution on three divisor classes is the product of their intersection numbers with \(C\). An alternative algebraic product agrees on the entire fibre-marked tube and all the traces of multiplication by each single state at this order. On a particular triple it gives one where the geometric count gives zero. The three-boundary relative invariant chooses between the two products. [The three-state measurement on a K3 surface](#ch15-a-cyclic-product-that-all-these-traces-can-miss)

Here one can count the lost information exactly. With the ordinary cup product, unit, pairing, cap scalars, fibre-marked operator and first multiplication traces held fixed, the possible graded commutative, cyclic first-order products have \(1750\) independent undetected coefficients. A specified collection of \(1750\) scalar readings on states of zero self-intersection recovers them all. No smaller collection of fixed linear readings separates this space. Whether an independent physical preparation produces those states is a separate question. The closed count has another description by stable pairs, maps from the structure sheaf to a pure one-dimensional sheaf with finite-length cokernel. The primitive counts in the chosen variables agree as rational functions. The closed counting function also has a finite geometric check. On a smooth genus-two curve, evaluate the fifth powers of holomorphic differentials at its six Weierstrass points. The determinant changes sign when two marked points are exchanged, and its square, with a fixed universal normalization, is the weight-ten Igusa form on the Jacobian. This supplies a check on the closed number independent of the three-state measurement. [Recovering the compact product](#ch15-a-cyclic-product-that-all-these-traces-can-miss)

There is a further requirement before a trace can be interpreted as quantum probabilities. The expectation of an operator followed by its adjoint must be nonnegative. Arithmetic supplies an exact test of the distinction. Summing functions over the integers defines a geometric space on which the trace of an operator gives the Weil formula relating prime powers to zeros of the Riemann zeta function. A positive representation accounts for precisely the zeros on the critical line, each with its multiplicity. It gives the same trace on every test exactly if the Riemann hypothesis holds. Apply the same quadratic test to one specified smooth pulse plus a copy translated by \(\log n\). Eventual nonnegativity of those readings is already equivalent to that hypothesis. On the disk positivity came from the energy of the physical field. On a three-dimensional filling the integral over the fields must supply the state. [A fixed translate test for positivity](#ch16-fixed-shape-translates)

In the arithmetic construction integer summation has closed image. In the stated Mellin transform space its image consists precisely of the functions vanishing to the full multiplicity at every zero of the completed zeta function. The continuous dual sees the corresponding derivatives. On a separate weighted Hilbert quotient, smoothing gives trace-class operations and a proper trace ideal. For test functions of exponential decay rate \(a>1/2\), choose a Hilbert strip of width parameter \(s\) with \(1/2<s<\min(a,1)\). Translation by a nonzero real logarithmic distance on this quotient has an entire annulus as its spectrum, so an equivalent norm cannot make it unitary. For the Weil functional, the prime-and-real-place expression already realized as a trace, Weil positivity can be proved for every square-integrable test supported in an interval of width at most \(31/10\), with an explicit strictly positive lower bound. The translated Weil test asks about the same pulse at separations extending beyond every fixed window. Even a full trace would leave a local question at a prime. At finite arithmetic jet height, a Frobenius lift and a normal derivative survive before evaluating at scalar points. A local field realization must preserve those operations, including their behaviour at the collision. [Arithmetic traces and their local limits](#ch16-a-positive-representation-and-its-exact-missing-remainder)

In a field theory the normalization of a filling may itself vary with the source. Its amplitudes then take values in a one-dimensional space, the determinant line. A heat calculation on the original quadratic fields of the solid torus constructs this line locally for small reflected sources with a spectral gap. After the divergent terms have been subtracted, the finite part gives a nonzero section relative to a chosen reference. It permits comparison at nearby sources. To obtain an absolute sewing law one still has to identify the section produced by an independently prepared geometric filling. [The local vacuum line](#ch11-original-coefficient-heat-and-a-based-local-vacuum-line)

On a fixed solid torus there is also a result with the mode cutoff removed. In the quadratic theory, for a sufficiently small smooth source with the prescribed boundary conditions and a smooth solution of its field equations, the finite integrals converge to a normalized Gaussian on the ordinary fields. Pair contractions give the correlations involving anticommuting fields as well. Even here the absolute cutting law remains open. Each half of a geometric cut must prepare a state independently, and their amplitudes, including their phases, must be compared in the same line. For gravity with interactions the comparison must survive the higher terms in the action. Perturb the source in each half. Pairing the two states should give both the joint response of the whole filling and its amplitude when both probes are removed. [The gravitational filling and its cutting law](#problem-gravitational-cap)

abstract:
Which probes can couple consistently to a boundary theory, and how do their operations act when two probes are joined? For an ordinary Lie symmetry the consistency equation gives representations of its enveloping algebra. Joining probes supplies the coproduct. In a marked one-variable boundary factorisation, the first nonzero higher product records the cubic or quartic bulk interaction. Identifying an independently prepared bulk theory also requires its action on the admitted boundary conditions and its unnormalised amplitudes under cutting.

A contour on a surface can measure more than the charge it encloses. Let \(J(z)\,dz\) be a holomorphic current in a coordinate disk. Suppose that two insertions of this current have the singular product
\[
J(z)J(w)\sim\frac{\kappa\,\mathbf 1}{(z-w)^2}.
\]
Here \(\mathbf 1\) is the vacuum field, \(\kappa\) is the level, and the two sides have the same polar part at \(z=w\). Integrate around \(w\) with a holomorphic weight \(f\). The residue of \(f(z)J(z)J(w)\,dz\) is \(\kappa f'(w)\mathbf 1\). A constant weight gives zero. The weight \(f(z)=z-w\) measures \(\kappa\). Replacing the two fields by a value at coincidence would lose the quantity the contour measures. [The free current](#heisenberg-current)

For three fields in a fixed order there are two ways to make successive binary collisions. One brings \(a\) to \(b\) and their product to \(c\), the other brings \(b\) to \(c\) first. Each prescription starts near its own diagonal in the space of three marked points. On a domain where both can be compared, write their products as \((ab)c\) and \(a(bc)\). When the fields form a cochain complex with differential \(d\), the comparison itself can be an operation. For closed inputs a degree-minus-one operation \(H\) gives
\[
dH(a,b,c)=(ab)c-a(bc).
\]
Thus the products agree on cohomology. A fourth field can be multiplied with \(H(a,b,c)\), so the choice of \(H\) still enters the next calculation. The five parenthesizations of four fields form a pentagon. Its two paths must be related by a further homotopy. An \(A_\infty\) multiplication keeps these operations and their compatibility at every number of inputs.

What makes this multiplication *chiral* is the geometry on which it acts. On a smooth complex algebraic curve \(X\), use complexes of right algebraic \(\mathcal D\)-modules on each \(X^n\). Their underlying sheaves are quasi-coherent, differential operators act in the marked positions, and the complexes have compatible extraordinary pullbacks along the diagonals that merge consecutive labels. The word \(1,\ldots,n\) records the order of multiplication. A cut after \(p\) separates two blocks. It is available on the open set \(U_{p,n-p}\) where each point of the first block is distinct from every point of the second. Points within a block may coincide. In the ordered word model, form the *bar construction* \(BA\) of an augmented coherent multiplication \(A\). It records strings of inputs and applies the products and their homotopies to consecutive entries. On degree-zero elements of the augmentation ideal of an ordinary associative algebra its product differential sends \([a|b|c]\) to \([ab|c]-[a|bc]\). The next differential gives the difference of the two triple products. For an associative chiral algebra in this model, cutting the string gives an equivalence on the separating open. Writing \(q=n-p\) and using \(\boxtimes\) for derived external tensor product, the factorization condition is
\[
(BA)_n|_{U_{p,q}}\xrightarrow{\simeq}\bigl((BA)_p\boxtimes(BA)_q\bigr)|_{U_{p,q}}.
\]

How much of the multiplication survives the passage to cuts? Give the empty configuration coefficient \(\mathbb C\), with its specified augmentation on the algebra and coaugmentation on the coalgebra. The reduced coefficients then have positive arity. A word of length \(n\) admits at most \(n\) nonempty blocks, so the iterated reduced constructions terminate at each arity. For a smooth separated algebraic curve of finite type, the resulting inverse theorem concerns the sequence of coefficient complexes. Bar and *cobar* are inverse equivalences between connected augmented algebras and connected counital coaugmented coalgebras for consecutive cuts, with their full derived spaces of maps. For a factorizing coalgebra the reduced three-input cobar coefficient vanishes wherever \(z_1\ne z_3\). Along \(z_1=z_3\), its support depends on the coalgebra. To carry the construction through a collision, observe that a cut inside a block of labels being identified disappears, while a cut between two such blocks descends to the corresponding cut of the shorter word. A comparison with fields constructed from a different theory must in addition identify their vacuum, translations and collision operations. [Recovering the algebra from cuts](#ch05-ordered-cuts-give-a-finite-geometric-bar-construction)

A different question arises when a symmetry acts on two independently prepared systems. Which current acts on their tensor product? If \(J_1\) and \(J_2\) have levels \(\kappa_1,\kappa_2\) and their mixed product is regular, their sum has double-pole coefficient \(\kappa_1+\kappa_2\). Writing \(H_\kappa\) for the algebra of a free current of level \(\kappa\), the simultaneous action comes from
\[
\begin{aligned}
H_{\kappa_1+\kappa_2}&\longrightarrow H_{\kappa_1}\otimes H_{\kappa_2},\\
J&\longmapsto J_1\otimes\mathbf1+\mathbf1\otimes J_2 .
\end{aligned}
\]
The direction and levels of this map are forced by the double pole. A unital field map from \(H_\kappa\) to the scalars would have to preserve it, so the regularity of scalar fields would force \(\kappa=0\). The augmentation at the empty configuration in the bar theorem belongs to the geometric coefficient system. In a chiral quantum group the coproduct must preserve the field products, give compatible actions on three systems and respect exchange when their positions move. These requirements concern the tensor product of systems. Cutting a string in the bar construction alone supplies no such action.

There is a class in which this compatibility is a theorem. Take a Hopf algebra over \(\mathbb C\) with bijective antipode and a translation \(T\) that is both a derivation and a coderivation and satisfies \(\varepsilon T=0\), where \(\varepsilon\) is its counit. A unitary spectral coquasitriangular form \(\rho_z\) pairs two inputs in Laurent polynomials in their separation \(z\). It is multiplicative against the coproduct, differentiates under translation, and implements an exchange whose reverse is its inverse. For Hopf automorphisms \(\eta,\theta\) preserving the translation and the form, these data construct a field algebra \(V_\eta\) at each such level \(\eta\). Writing \(\Delta\) for the Hopf coproduct, the maps for combining levels form a coassociative family
\[
D_{\eta,\theta}=(\theta\otimes 1)\Delta:
V_{\eta\theta}\longrightarrow V_\eta\boxtimes_\rho V_\theta .
\]
The tensor product on the right uses \(\rho\) when a field in one factor passes a field in the other. With that contraction included, applying \(D\) to a product gives the product of the images, with its full dependence on \(z\). Exchanging the product with a third field is the composite of the two exchanges with its factors. This is the field hexagon. [The spectral field and coproduct](#ch12-a-spectral-construction-of-products-and-coproducts)

Holography asks which operations and states on a boundary can be obtained from a field theory in the space it bounds. In a free holomorphic–topological half-space, a test field supported strictly above the boundary has zero boundary restriction. Multiply it by a boundary input before integrating out the transverse fields and there can be a contraction. On polynomial current states \(f(p_1,p_2,\ldots)\), a test tuned to harmonic \(j\) acts by \(\partial f/\partial p_j\) at quantum current level one. Each occurrence of \(p_j\) gives one possible contraction. This computes an interior action on the boundary cochains. To determine a state one must also specify its preparation.

In the free abelian Chern–Simons half-space theory at level one, put two oriented charge lines of strengths \(a,-a\) above the points \(r,0\) of a marked unit disk, with \(a\) real and \(0<r<1\). Use constant framing, subtract self-contractions, and take the prescribed limit of outgoing separations in a fixed real direction. The current on an outer contour sees \(a/(z-r)-a/z\). The unweighted residue is zero. Weighting by \(z^n\), as in the first contour calculation, gives the eigenvalue \(ar^n\) of the positive current mode for \(n\ge1\). Independently, take a real harmonic field \(\phi=h+\bar h\) on the disk with constant mode zero, and write \(h(z)=\sum_{n\ge1}Z_nz^n/n\). Weight its Gaussian law by \(\exp(a\phi(r))\) and normalize. Completing the square gives \(\mathbb E Z_n=ar^n\) and \(\mathbb E|Z_n-ar^n|^2=n\). The squared modulus of the normalized ray wavefunction, multiplied by the vacuum Gaussian density, gives this same law on every finite set of harmonics and hence on the full sequence. [Neutral rays and a sourced disk](#ch11-neutral-ray-pair)

Propagating through a cylinder of length \(L\ge0\) damps harmonic \(n\) by \(q^n\), \(q=e^{-L}\). The normalized overlap of the prepared state with its propagated state is \(\bigl((1-r^2)/(1-qr^2)\bigr)^{a^2}\) on both sides. The factor \(r^{-a^2}\) in the ray amplitude cancels from this measurement. An absolute cutting law must keep the vacuum amplitude as well.

On a solid torus with fixed metric and density, a quadratic gravitational model admits a normalized calculation after removal of the mode cutoff. Take a torus multiplier of modulus strictly between zero and one, nonzero coupling, positive \(\hbar\), and a sufficiently small smooth integrable source of zero normal trace admitting a smooth solution of the Ward equations. The cutoff even fields converge in mean square and almost surely in a space of distributions. Their limit has a Gaussian law, and graded Wick contraction gives the moments involving odd fields. In a reflected realization with a spectral gap, smooth source bounds and finite action integrals, heat regularization gives a nonzero local section of the vacuum line, the one-dimensional space in which the unnormalized vacuum amplitude takes its values. This determines how the normalization varies near a reference. The absolute geometric cutting law remains open already in this quadratic model. Each geometric half must prepare its own state, and pairing those states must reproduce the uncut amplitude, including its phase and its response to insertions. For interacting quantum gravity that comparison must also respect the interaction terms. A common phase of the entire amplitude cancels in every probability. A relative phase between components of a single normalized state can survive, even when the occupations of its modes have identical distributions in two preparations.
